fact: Many decisions arise via the accumulation of noisy evidence to a threshold or bound.
source_span: Many decisions are thought to arise via the accumulation of noisy evidence to a threshold or bound .
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the fundamental decision-making mechanism studied in the article.

fact: In perception, the accumulation of noisy evidence explains how stimulus strength affects decision speed, accuracy, and confidence.
source_span: In perception , the mechanism explains the effect of stimulus strength , characterized by signal-to-noise ratio , on decision speed , accuracy and confidence .
selection_reasoning: This fact provides context for why the study focuses on noise and its effects on decision variables.

fact: An increase in noise is predicted to lead to faster decisions, reduced accuracy, and paradoxically higher confidence.
source_span: An increase in noise should lead to faster decisions , reduced accuracy and , paradoxically , higher confidence .
selection_reasoning: This is a key theoretical prediction that the study aims to test.

fact: The study introduced a novel sensory manipulation that mimics adding unbiased noise to motion-selective regions of visual cortex.
source_span: To test these predictions , we introduce a novel sensory manipulation that mimics the addition of unbiased noise to motion-selective regions of visual cortex , which we verified with neuronal recordings from macaque areas MT/MST .
selection_reasoning: This describes the main experimental approach used to test the theoretical predictions.

fact: Neuronal recordings from macaque areas MT/MST verified the sensory manipulation increased noise in motion-selective visual cortex.
source_span: which we verified with neuronal recordings from macaque areas MT/MST .
selection_reasoning: This supports the validity of the noise manipulation method.

fact: In both humans and monkeys, increasing noise induced faster decisions and greater confidence with minimal impairment of accuracy.
source_span: For both humans and monkeys , increasing the noise induced faster decisions and greater confidence over a range of stimuli for which accuracy was minimally impaired .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal empirical finding confirming key model predictions.

fact: The magnitude of the effects of noise on decision speed and confidence matched predictions of a bounded evidence accumulation model.
source_span: The magnitude of the effects was in agreement with predictions of a bounded evidence accumulation model .
selection_reasoning: This links the experimental results to the theoretical framework.

fact: Decisions that combine information from different sources or over time serve as a model of cognitive function because they are not hardwired or reflexive but experimentally tractable.
source_span: Decisions that combine information from different sources or across time are of special interest to neuroscience because they serve as a model of cognitive function . These decisions are not hard wired or reflexive , yet they are experimentally tractable .
selection_reasoning: This explains the significance of studying such decisions in neuroscience.

fact: Psychologists have identified three key observables in decision formation: choice accuracy, reaction time, and decision confidence.
source_span: Psychologists have long sought to understand how the process of decision formation gives rise to three key observables ... First there is the choice itself ... Second , there is the time it takes to reach a decision ... Third , decisions are often accompanied by a graded degree of belief ... referred to as decision confidence ...
selection_reasoning: This background clarifies the main behavioral measures the study addresses.

fact: Bounded evidence accumulation models explain choice, reaction time, and confidence by modeling decision variables that accumulate evidence until reaching a threshold.
source_span: The family of bounded evidence accumulation models ... offers one such framework for linking choice , reaction time and confidence ... The decision terminates when the accumulated evidence for one alternative , termed a decision variable ( DV ) , reaches a threshold or bound , thereby determining both the choice and the decision time . Confidence in the decision derives from a mapping between the DV and the probability that a decision based on this DV will be correct .
selection_reasoning: This describes the theoretical framework underlying the study's hypotheses.

fact: Noise in momentary evidence causes the decision variable to fluctuate, influencing reaction time and confidence especially when signal-to-noise ratio is low.
source_span: The noisiness of the momentary evidence causes the DV to wander from its starting point ... Noise is the main determinant of both RT and confidence when signal-to-noise is low , that is when choices are more stochastic ( less accurate ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the role of noise in decision dynamics relevant to the study.

fact: If noise is selectively increased without changing the mean evidence, bounded accumulation predicts lower accuracy with strong evidence, faster reaction times with weak evidence, and increased confidence with weak evidence.
source_span: Specifically , were it possible to leave unchanged the expectation of each sample of momentary evidence while boosting the noise associated with it , then the bounded accumulation of the noisier samples should lead to ( i ) lower accuracy when the expectation of the momentary evidence is strong , ( ii ) faster reaction times when the momentary evidence is weak , and ( iii ) increased confidence when the momentary evidence is weak .
selection_reasoning: This outlines the specific testable predictions motivating the experimental manipulation.

fact: The study introduced a method to selectively increase the variance of neural evidence without changing its mean by manipulating the volatility of motion information in a random dot motion display.
source_span: We therefore sought a method to manipulate the variance associated with the neural representation of momentary evidence without affecting its mean. We achieved this with a manipulation of the motion information in a random dot motion (RDM) display, by adding a second level of randomness which increased its volatility but was unbiased with respect to the strength and direction of motion evidence.
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the key methodological innovation central to the study's main question about how noise affects decision-making.

fact: Neurons in the middle temporal (MT) and medial superior temporal (MST) areas of the macaque visual cortex represent momentary motion evidence and were used to verify the effects of the volatility manipulation.
source_span: We verified that the manipulation has the desired properties by recording from direction selective neurons in the middle temporal (MT) and medial superior temporal (MST) areas of the macaque visual cortex. Neurons in these areas are known to represent the momentary evidence in tasks identical to those in our study.
selection_reasoning: This fact provides important biological context and validation of the manipulation at the neural level, supporting the study's claims.

fact: The volatility manipulation increased the variance of motion evidence without affecting its mean motion strength in both the stimulus and neural responses.
source_span: For all motion strengths, the mean (upper) is not affected by the volatility manipulation, whereas the variance is larger in the high volatility condition. ... The volatility manipulation produced a small increase in the average firing rate at the low coherences ... The variance parallels the mean, but volatility has a more marked effect on variance at weak motion strengths.
selection_reasoning: This fact states the principal finding that the manipulation selectively increased noise (variance) while keeping mean evidence constant, which is central to the study's hypothesis.

fact: The study tested how increased noise in momentary evidence influences choice accuracy, reaction time, and confidence in both monkeys and humans.
source_span: We then used the volatility manipulation to test the influence of noise on the three observables of choice behavior—accuracy, RT and confidence—in monkeys and humans.
selection_reasoning: This fact summarizes the main experimental goal and the behavioral measures assessed, linking neural manipulation to behavior.

fact: Previous methods to increase neural noise, such as transcranial magnetic stimulation or cortical microstimulation, inferred effects from behavior but did not directly characterize neural signals underlying decision formation.
source_span: A dissociation between accuracy and confidence led Rahnev et al. (2012) to conclude that transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) increased the neural noise associated with the representation of a visual pattern ... However, characterization of these effects of TMS and μStim was inferred from behavior. Similarly, psychophysical studies that attempted to increase the noise ... did not characterize the influence of these manipulations on the neural signals that the brain accumulates to form a decision.
selection_reasoning: This fact provides motivation for the study by highlighting limitations of prior approaches and the need for direct neural characterization.

fact: The standard random dot motion stimulus has a fixed motion coherence for the duration of a trial, whereas the high volatility condition varies the motion coherence randomly on each video frame around a fixed mean.
source_span: In the standard RDM, the coherence, c, is fixed for the duration of an experimental trial ... Here we introduce a second layer of variability, wherein the mean of c is fixed for the duration of a trial but the value of c varies randomly from video frame to video frame ... We will refer to trials that employ this doubly stochastic RDM as the 'high volatility' condition and those that use the standard RDM as 'low volatility'.
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the key experimental manipulation at a high level, necessary to understand the study design.

fact: The variance of neural responses to motion stimuli increases more under high volatility conditions, especially at low motion strengths.
source_span: The variance of the neural response is known to scale approximately linearly with firing rate ( Tolhurst et al . , 1983; Vogels et al . , 1989; Geisler and Albrecht , 1997; Shadlen and Newsome , 1998 ) . Thus the variance curves in Figure 2C ( lower panel ) parallel the means . The high volatility condition adds to the variance in a manner that is exaggerated at the low motion strengths , consistent with the motion energy analysis above .
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights a key finding about how stimulus volatility affects neural variability, which is central to understanding neural processing of motion and decision-making.

fact: The firing rate of direction-selective neurons in cortical areas MT/MST increases linearly with motion strength in the preferred direction and decreases less steeply in the anti-preferred direction, forming a bilinear function.
source_span: As previously shown ( Britten et al . , 1993 ) , the firing rate of MT neurons increases linearly , on average , as a function of motion strength in the neuron’s preferred direction ( c > 0 , Figure 2C , upper panel , blue trace ) . The firing rate decreases linearly , but less steeply , as a function of motion strength in the anti-preferred direction ( c < 0 ) , giving rise to a bilinear function .
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the neural coding of motion strength, which is fundamental to the study's investigation of neural responses under different volatility conditions.

fact: High volatility stimuli increase the variance of motion energy compared to low volatility stimuli, especially at low motion strengths where the distribution of coherence spans positive and negative values.
source_span: A more systematic analysis of the motion energy , displayed in Figure 2B , reveals that the mean is identical for low and high volatility stimuli , for all motion strengths ( upper panel ) , whereas the variance is larger for the high volatility stimuli ( lower panel ) . ... Note that the effect is strongest at the low coherences , where the distribution of c in the high volatility condition spans both positive and negative values .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the stimulus property manipulation that underlies the experimental design and its impact on sensory input variability.

fact: The momentary evidence used by monkeys to guide motion discrimination decisions is represented by the difference in firing rates between two pools of neurons preferring opposite motion directions.
source_span: We assume that the momentary evidence is the difference between the average firing rates from two pools of neurons with direction preferences for the two opposite directions ( e . g . , right-preferring minus left-preferring ) ( Shadlen et al . , 1996; Ditterich et al . , 2003;
selection_reasoning: This fact defines the key neural mechanism underlying decision formation, which is central to the study's main question.

fact: The visual system blurs rapidly displayed random dot motion stimuli over time, creating the perception of more dots than are actually present simultaneously.
source_span: The construction of the RDM we use is in video frames displayed every 1/75 of a second . The visual system blurs these images over time , leading for example to the illusion that many more dots are present simultaneously than are actually displayed .
selection_reasoning: This background fact helps explain the nature of the stimulus and why it is relevant for studying motion perception.

fact: An established motion filter applied to the stimuli extracts a time-blurred motion signal that approximates the firing rates of direction-selective neurons in primate visual cortex.
source_span: The right panel of Figure 2A applies an established motion filter ( Adelson and Bergen , 1985 ) to the example movies parameterized by the low and high volatility traces shown in the left panel ( see also Video 1 ) . The filter extracts a time-blurred motion signal that provides a reasonable approximation to the firing rates of direction selective neurons in the primate visual cortex ( Britten et al . , 1993; Rust et al . , 2006; Hedges et al . , 2011 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes a key method used to relate stimulus properties to neural responses, supporting the study's approach.

fact: The mean motion energy is identical for low and high volatility stimuli across all motion strengths.
source_span: A more systematic analysis of the motion energy , displayed in Figure 2B , reveals that the mean is identical for low and high volatility stimuli , for all motion strengths ( upper panel ) ,
selection_reasoning: This fact establishes that volatility affects variance but not mean motion energy, which is important for interpreting neural and behavioral effects.

fact: The study investigated how changes in the variance of momentary sensory evidence affect decision speed, accuracy, and confidence in a motion direction discrimination task.
source_span: In what follows we attempt to ascertain whether a change in the variance of the momentary evidence , introduced by our volatility manipulation , affects decision speed , accuracy , and confidence in accordance with the predictions of bounded evidence accumulation .
selection_reasoning: This fact states the main research question and motivation, which is central to the abstract-level summary.

fact: One monkey and three human subjects performed a task requiring them to decide the net direction of motion in a dynamic random dot display by making a saccadic eye movement to one of two targets.
source_span: One monkey ( monkey W ) and three humans were required to decide between two possible directions of motion and , when ready , to indicate their decision by looking to one of two targets ( Figure 3A ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the key experimental subjects and task, important for understanding the methods at a high level.

fact: Stronger motion coherence led to faster and more accurate choices in both high and low volatility conditions.
source_span: For both high and low volatility conditions , stronger motion led to faster and more accurate choices .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal behavioral finding that establishes the expected effect of motion strength on performance.

fact: Increasing stimulus volatility increased the variance of momentary sensory evidence, especially at low motion strengths, without substantially changing the mean evidence.
source_span: From these complementary analyses of stimulus and neural response , we conclude that the volatility manipulation has negligible effects on the expectation of momentary evidence and more substantial effects on the variance , especially at weak motion strengths .
selection_reasoning: This fact links the stimulus manipulation to its neural and computational effect, which is central to the study's hypothesis.

fact: High volatility decreased reaction times, particularly at the weakest motion strengths, across all subjects including the monkey and humans.
source_span: The main effect of high volatility was to decrease RTs , particularly at the weakest motion strengths ( Figure 3B , bottom row , red ) . This effect was robust for all three human subjects and the monkey ( Equation 16 , all p<0 . 03 , t-test , H0: β2=0 ) .
selection_reasoning: This is a key behavioral result demonstrating the effect of volatility on decision speed, a core claim.

fact: The effect of high volatility on accuracy was subtle and not statistically reliable for individual subjects in the reaction time task but was significant when pooling data across subjects and including confidence tasks.
source_span: The manipulation affected the accuracy only subtly , and this was not statistically reliable for individual subjects in the RT task ( Figure 3B , top row; for the four subjects: p=[0 . 35 , 0 . 65 , 0 . 2 , 0 . 26] , Equation 17 , likelihood-ratio test ) . However , there was a significant effect of volatility on accuracy when pooling data across subjects and including data from the confidence tasks described below ( Equation 18 , p<0 . 0005 , likelihood ratio test , H0: β2=0; see also Figure 3—figure supplement 1 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact qualifies the effect of volatility on accuracy, important for interpreting the behavioral impact.

fact: The momentary evidence used for decision-making was modeled as the difference in average firing rates between two pools of neurons selective for opposite motion directions.
source_span: We assume that the momentary evidence is the difference between the average firing rates from two pools of neurons with direction preferences for the two opposite directions ( e . g . , right-preferring minus left-preferring ) ( Shadlen et al . , 1996; Ditterich et al . , 2003; Hanks et al . , 2006 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact provides a key mechanistic assumption underlying the neural basis of the decision variable.

fact: Neuronal correlations within pools reduce the variance of the population response, but the variance saturates with a modest number of neurons due to these correlations.
source_span: Assuming a population of correlated neurons , the variance of the population mean differs from that of a single neuron by a multiplicative constant . For large pools , the variance is reduced to roughly rσ2 , where r is the average pairwise spike-count correlation for neurons within the pool ... An important implication of such correlation is that the beneficial effects of pooling saturate with modest number of neurons ( e . g . , 50–100; [Zohary et al . , 1994; Shadlen et al . , 1996] ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains a key neural mechanism affecting the variance of momentary evidence, relevant to interpreting the stimulus manipulation.

fact: Subjects decided the net direction of motion in a dynamic random dot display by making a saccadic eye movement to the corresponding target.
source_span: Subjects reported their decision by making a saccadic eye movement to the right ( left ) target for rightward ( leftward ) motion .
selection_reasoning: This describes the core behavioral task used to measure decision-making, essential background for understanding the study.

fact: High volatility in the motion stimulus had only weak effects on choice accuracy but shortened reaction times, especially at low motion strengths.
source_span: High volatility had only weak effects on accuracy ( upper ) but shortened the reaction times for all subjects ( lower ) , particularly at the low motion strengths .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding linking stimulus volatility to decision speed and accuracy, central to the study's claims.

fact: Decisions are consistent with a bounded evidence accumulation model where increased volatility increases the variance of momentary evidence.
source_span: The pattern of results in Figure 3B is consistent with the hypothesis that decisions are made when an accumulation of noisy evidence reaches a bound . Indeed , the smooth curves are fits of this model to the data , where the variance of the momentary evidence is the only parameter that we allowed to change between conditions of high and low volatility .
selection_reasoning: This provides the key mechanistic interpretation of the behavioral data, linking volatility effects to evidence accumulation.

fact: Increased volatility accelerates the dispersion of the decision variable, leading to faster reaction times especially at weak motion strengths.
source_span: The important point is that by increasing noise , the volatility manipulation accelerates the dispersion of the decision variable away from its expected value and nearer the termination bounds , hence faster RT .
selection_reasoning: This explains the mechanism by which volatility affects decision speed, a core scientific claim.

fact: Confidence in a decision can be formalized as the conditional probability of a correct choice given the accumulated evidence and elapsed decision time.
source_span: Confidence refers to the belief that a decision one is about to make ( or has just made ) is likely to be correct . In the framework of bounded evidence accumulation , it can be formalized as the conditional probability of a correct choice given the state of the DV , which comprises the accumulated evidence and elapsed decision time .
selection_reasoning: This defines confidence in the context of the study, necessary background for understanding subsequent findings.

fact: Increased volatility is predicted to increase confidence at low motion coherences by accelerating the decision variable away from neutral values.
source_span: Increased volatility should affect confidence because it mimics an increase in the diffusion rate . At low coherences in particular , its main effect on the DV is to accelerate its exodus away from neutral ( probability correct = 0 . 5 ) to more extreme values . Therefore , we predicted that volatility would increase confidence at low coherences , for the same reason that it speeds the RT .
selection_reasoning: This is a key hypothesis linking volatility to confidence, central to the study's main question.

fact: A monkey was trained on a motion discrimination task with post-decision wagering, allowing it to opt out for a smaller but certain reward after viewing the motion stimulus.
source_span: Monkey D was trained on a motion discrimination task with post-decision wagering ( Kiani and Shadlen , 2009 ) ( PDW; Figure 4A ) . The monkey had to decide between two opposite directions of motion and report its decision after a memory delay . On half of the trials , the monkey had the opportunity to opt out of reporting the direction choice and to select instead a smaller but certain reward .
selection_reasoning: This describes a key experimental method used to measure confidence behaviorally in a non-human primate.

fact: High volatility motion stimuli were introduced on a random half of trials after extensive training with low volatility stimuli in the monkey post-decision wagering task.
source_span: After extensive experience with the standard RDM ( >100 , 000 trials; low volatility condition ) , we introduced the high volatility RDM on a random half of the trials .
selection_reasoning: This details the experimental manipulation critical for testing the effect of volatility on decision and confidence.

fact: The study investigated how stimulus volatility affects decision confidence in a motion discrimination task.
source_span: The main question we wished to address is whether the high volatility condition would elicit fewer sure-bet choices, consistent with greater confidence.
selection_reasoning: This fact states the core research question motivating the study.

fact: Monkeys performed a motion discrimination task where they indicated motion direction and could opt for a sure-bet option that gave a small but certain reward.
source_span: The monkey viewed the motion display for random duration, controlled by the computer, followed by a memory-delay period. When the fixation point was extinguished, the monkey indicated the net direction of motion by making an eye movement to a left or right choice target in order to receive a liquid reward, if correct. On a random half of trials, the monkey was presented a third ‘sure bet’ option (red target) during the delay period, which if chosen resulted in a small but certain reward.
selection_reasoning: This describes the key behavioral task and the sure-bet option used to measure decision confidence.

fact: High stimulus volatility increased the monkey’s confidence, as shown by a higher proportion of trials in which the monkey waived the sure-bet option and chose the riskier direction choice.
source_span: As shown in Figure 4B (lower panel), the proportion of trials the monkey decided to waive the sure-bet option (deciding instead for a riskier direction choice) was greater on the high volatility trials (Equation 19, p<10–6, likelihood-ratio test). Thus, high volatility increased the monkey’s confidence, and did so despite a negligible effect on accuracy (Figure 4B, upper).
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding linking volatility to increased confidence without affecting accuracy.

fact: Volatility had little effect on accuracy in the motion discrimination task for both monkeys and humans.
source_span: Volatility did not affect accuracy systematically (upper panels).
selection_reasoning: This clarifies that confidence changes were not due to changes in task accuracy, an important control.

fact: Monkeys made rational use of the sure-bet option by opting out more often when motion evidence was weak or stimulus duration was brief, improving accuracy on trials where they chose the direction decision.
source_span: In both low and high volatility conditions, the monkey made rational use of the sure bet, opting out more often for weaker motion (Equation 19, p<10–6, logistic regression) and for briefer stimuli (Equation 19, p<10–6, logistic regression). When the sure bet was offered but waived, choice accuracy was higher than when the sure bet was not offered (Equation 20, p<10–6, logistic regression).
selection_reasoning: This supports the interpretation that the sure-bet choice reflects trial-by-trial confidence based on evidence quality.

fact: Human participants also reported higher confidence for high volatility stimuli, especially at low motion coherence, despite no systematic change in accuracy.
source_span: The results from the human observers were similar to those from the monkey. ... They also reported higher confidence for the high volatility stimuli, and the effect was most apparent for the low coherence stimuli (Equation 21, p<0.0004, t-test).
selection_reasoning: This extends the main finding to humans, supporting generality and translational relevance.

fact: Participants reported their confidence on a continuous scale after viewing 200 ms of random dot motion with either low or high volatility.
source_span: The RDM (low or high volatility, randomly interleaved) was displayed for a fixed 200 ms on each trial, after which they reported the perceived direction of motion (left or right) and the confidence in their decision.
selection_reasoning: This describes the key human experimental method used to measure confidence.

fact: A single bounded accumulation model can explain how motion strength and volatility affect choice, accuracy, reaction time, and confidence in perceptual decisions.
source_span: Now we show how a single bounded accumulation model can account for the combined effect of motion strength and volatility on choice, accuracy and RT.
selection_reasoning: This fact summarizes the main modeling approach linking key variables to decision outcomes, central to the study's principal findings.

fact: In the bounded accumulation model, choice, reaction time, and confidence result from accumulating noisy momentary evidence until a decision bound is reached or the stimulus ends.
source_span: In the model, choice, RT and confidence result from the accumulation of noisy momentary evidence as a function of time, until the integral of the evidence (the decision variable, DV) reaches one of two bounds, or for the PDW and confidence tasks, until the stimulus is curtailed.
selection_reasoning: This fact provides a high-level description of the key method used to explain decision-making and confidence, important for understanding the study.

fact: The variance of momentary evidence increases with motion strength, and the difference in noise between volatility conditions is largest at zero coherence and decreases with stronger motion.
source_span: These analyses showed that (i) the variance of the momentary evidence increases with motion strength, and (ii) the difference in noise between volatility conditions is larger at 0% coherence and decays gradually for stronger motion.
selection_reasoning: This fact identifies a key empirical observation about how stimulus properties affect evidence variability, which is central to the model and findings.

fact: The model assumes that the brain has implicit knowledge of the accumulated evidence state, elapsed decision time, and how these map to the probability of making a correct choice to explain confidence judgments.
source_span: We assume that the brain has implicit knowledge of (i) the state of the accumulated evidence, (ii) the elapsed deliberation time, and (iii) the mapping of time and evidence to the probability of making a correct choice.
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the cognitive mechanism underlying confidence, a principal outcome of the study.

fact: Time matters for confidence because the same level of accumulated evidence corresponds to lower accuracy if it was accumulated over a longer time.
source_span: Time matters because the same level of accumulated evidence is associated with lower levels of accuracy if the evidence was accrued over longer periods of time.
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights an important insight about how decision time influences confidence, relevant to the study's conclusions.

fact: The model fits to human data show that time and accumulated evidence are the main determinants of confidence in perceptual choices, even when noise is experimentally controlled.
source_span: These predictions capture the trend well, supporting the notion that time and accumulated evidence are the main determinants of confidence in a perceptual choice, even when noise is under experimental control.
selection_reasoning: This fact states a principal finding validating the model's explanatory power for confidence judgments.

fact: The influence of motion strength and volatility on choice, reaction time, and confidence can be explained by a common bounded evidence accumulation mechanism across tasks and species.
source_span: The overall quality of the fits—across all tasks and both species—indicates that the influence of motion strength and volatility on choice, reaction time and confidence can be explained by a common mechanism of bounded evidence accumulation.
selection_reasoning: This fact summarizes the broad significance and generalizability of the study's main conclusion.

fact: Subjects do not appear to adjust their mapping between accumulated evidence and confidence based on the noisiness (volatility) of the stimulus.
source_span: We assume that subjects do not infer the noisiness of incoming evidence, or that if they do, they do not revise the mapping accordingly.
selection_reasoning: This fact addresses a key assumption about how confidence is computed, relevant to interpreting the findings.

fact: Subjects apply the same mapping between accumulated evidence and confidence regardless of stimulus volatility condition.
source_span: that subjects apply the same mapping between the accumulated evidence ( the DV ) and the probability that a decision rendered upon that evidence will be correct ( i . e . , confidence ) , regardless of the volatility condition .
selection_reasoning: This is a core finding about how confidence is computed across different volatility conditions, central to the study's main question.

fact: Models that assume subjects use separate mappings for high and low volatility conditions fit the data worse than models assuming a common mapping.
source_span: When fit to data , this two-map model produces visibly worse fits than the model that relies on a common map , despite having the same number of parameters ( Figure 6B; ∆BIC = 252 . 4 favoring the common-map model; see Table 2 for parameter fits ) .
selection_reasoning: This finding supports the conclusion that a single mapping explains confidence better than volatility-specific mappings, a principal result.

fact: Subjects do not appear to infer or adjust for the noisiness of incoming evidence in real time to change their confidence mapping.
source_span: Thus , we assume that subjects do not infer the noisiness of incoming evidence , or that if they do , they do not revise the mapping accordingly .
selection_reasoning: This addresses the study's main question about whether volatility is accounted for in confidence judgments.

fact: A model allowing gradual assessment of volatility during a trial found that volatility information accrual is very slow and confidence remains dominated by a common mapping.
source_span: For the second two-map model , the assessment of volatility is not instantaneous but evolves over the course of a trial . ... the rate estimated from the best fit is exceedingly slow . For example , after 1 s of viewing , the weight assigned to the appropriate volatility map is just 1% . In other words , the confidence is dominated by the common mapping , consistent with our assumption .
selection_reasoning: This finding further supports the conclusion that subjects do not rapidly adjust confidence based on volatility.

fact: Allowing different decision bounds for high and low volatility conditions did not improve model fits compared to a common bound model.
source_span: We also considered the possibility that subjects used different termination criteria ( bound heights ) on low and high volatility trials . ... This model was also inferior to the simpler common-map model ( ∆BIC = 127; see Table 2 for parameter fits ) .
selection_reasoning: This result supports the conclusion that decision strategies do not differ by volatility in this task.

fact: The study's volatility manipulation was validated and characterized using neural data from neurons representing momentary evidence for decisions and confidence.
source_span: The role of the neural data in this study was to validate and characterize the volatility manipulation in a population of neurons known to represent the momentary evidence used to inform decisions and confidence ( Salzman et al . , 1990; Ditterich
selection_reasoning: This provides key background and methodological context linking behavioral findings to neural evidence.

fact: The normative strategy for similar decision tasks would apply different mappings and bounds for different volatility conditions, but subjects in this study did not follow this strategy.
source_span: Indeed , the normative strategy for several model tasks , which approximate those in our study , would apply different bounds and mappings to the two volatility conditions ( see Appendix ) . The full normative solution for the tasks we used is not known . Hence , we do not know if our subjects performed suboptimally or if they were simply unable to identify the volatility conditions without adding additional costs ( e . g . , effort and/or time ) .
selection_reasoning: This highlights the significance and interpretation of the findings in the context of normative decision theory.

fact: The study used neural data from a population of neurons known to represent momentary evidence used to inform decisions and confidence.
source_span: The role of the neural data in this study was to validate and characterize the volatility manipulation in a population of neurons known to represent the momentary evidence used to inform decisions and confidence ( Salzman et al., 1990; Ditterich et al., 2003; Hanks et al., 2006; Fetsch et al., 2014 ).
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the biological basis and motivation for using neural data to study decision-making and confidence, which is central to the study.

fact: Trial-to-trial variation in the activity of neurons in MT/MST was indicative of the choice the monkey was about to make.
source_span: Consistent with earlier reports ( Britten et al., 1992 ), trial to trial variation in the activity of neurons in MT/MST were indicative of the choice that the monkey was about to make.
selection_reasoning: This is a key finding linking neural activity to behavioral choice, fundamental to the study's claims.

fact: Trial-to-trial variation in neural responses was more informative in the high volatility condition due to exaggerated variance in the motion display.
source_span: For both low and high volatility conditions, trial-to-trial variation in the neural response was reflected in the monkey’s choices. The fluctuations were more informative in the high volatility condition, presumably because they were induced by exaggerated variance in the motion display itself.
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the main experimental manipulation (volatility) and its effect on neural-behavioral correlation, central to the study.

fact: The time course of choice-related neural signals evolved with similar latencies in both low and high volatility conditions, matching the latency of the direction selective signal.
source_span: Notably, the time course of choice-related signals evolved with similar latencies in the low and high volatility conditions. The latencies were comparable to that of the direction selective signal itself.
selection_reasoning: This finding relates to the timing of neural signals underlying decision-making, a principal result.

fact: The influence of neural variation on choice declines over about 200 ms, consistent with the brain terminating some decisions before stimulus end.
source_span: The influence of neural variation declines over 200 ms, consistent with the idea that the brain terminates some decisions before the end of the stimulus presentation.
selection_reasoning: This fact provides insight into the temporal dynamics of decision-making, important for understanding the neural basis of choices.

fact: Trial-by-trial variation in neural activity was correlated with the decision to accept or waive a sure-bet option when it was offered.
source_span: The trial-by-trial variation in neural activity was also correlated with the decision to accept or waive the sure-bet option, when it was offered.
selection_reasoning: This links neural activity not only to choice but also to confidence-related decisions, a key aspect of the study.

fact: Ubiquitination is a eukaryotic post-translational modification involving a cascade of enzymes (E1, E2, E3) that attach ubiquitin to substrate proteins, regulating processes like immune signaling.

fact: Phase relations among neuronal groups contribute to selective routing of information and shape effective connectivity in the brain.

source_span: Up to 60% of cells in the anterior thalamus are classical head direction (HD) cells... The preferred directions of all cells in the HD ensemble span the full range of compass directions.
selection_reasoning: This background fact is necessary to understand the significance of modeling HD inputs to LR neurons.

fact: Synaptic depression of head direction (HD) ensemble inputs introduces an angular head speed signal into the low-rheobase (LR) neuron population in the retrosplenial granular cortex (RSG).
source_span: Taken together, these results suggest that synaptic depression of HD ensemble inputs introduces an angular head speed signal into the LR population, producing neurons that are more responsive during faster head turns, and potentially supporting the spatial orientation encoding functions attributed to the RSG.
selection_reasoning: This fact links synaptic mechanisms to the encoding of angular head speed, a core finding relevant to spatial orientation and the function of the studied brain region.

fact: Anterior thalamic head direction cells display anticipatory firing, becoming most active before the animal faces the cell’s preferred direction, with a mean anticipatory time interval (ATI) of 25–50 ms.
source_span: Anterior thalamic HD cells display anticipatory firing (Blair et al., 1997), a phenomenon where an HD cell becomes most active at a fixed time interval before the animal is facing that cell’s preferred direction... In anterior thalamus, the mean ATI has been reported as 25–50 ms (Taube, 2010).
selection_reasoning: This background fact defines anticipatory firing and ATI, which are central to understanding the study’s investigation of timing effects on speed coding.

fact: Increasing the anticipatory time interval (ATI) of HD cells improves the timing and quality of angular head speed coding by LR neurons, reducing latency and enhancing tuning.
source_span: Increasing ATI from 0 ms (no anticipation by the HD cell) to higher values (HD cell firing prior to facing the preferred HD) improved the lag between LR firing rate and angular head speed, with larger ATIs resulting in shorter latency between the head movement and LR coding of that angular head speed... larger ATIs also improved the angular head speed tuning of LR neurons independent of lag.
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding showing how anticipatory firing enhances the neural representation of head speed, a key mechanistic insight.

fact: Analytical modeling shows that synaptic depression of HD cell inputs onto LR cells leads to angular head speed coding, and anticipatory firing compensates for integration lag, enabling near-perfect speed coding.
source_span: Our analysis allowed us to mathematically derive that LR activity should encode head speed with depressing synapses from simplified HD cells... anticipatory firing compensates for the lag introduced by integration time, leading to a theoretical parameter regime for which postsynaptic speed coding can be essentially perfect.
selection_reasoning: This theoretical result supports and explains the simulation findings, providing mechanistic understanding of the coding process.

fact: Postsynaptic LR neuron activity at lower rotational speeds is proportional to the square of head speed, explaining the parabolic shape of the speed-firing rate curve.
source_span: Our analysis showed that postsynaptic activity, at least at lower rotational speeds, is proportional to the square of head speed, thereby explaining the concave-up, parabolic shape of the speed-firing rate curve.
selection_reasoning: This fact explains a key characteristic of the neural response curve, linking firing rate to head speed quantitatively.

fact: LR neurons receive heterogeneous inputs from HD cells with varying preferred directions, resulting in a tradeoff between encoding head direction and head speed.
source_span: We found that single cell activity in the LR population could encode both head direction and head speed, but there was a clear tradeoff between the two types of information... This tradeoff between directional versus speed encoding was explained by the level of heterogeneity in the presynaptic preferred direction distribution.
selection_reasoning: This finding reveals how input diversity shapes the conjunctive coding properties of LR neurons, a key insight into their functional role.

fact: LR cells in the granular retrosplenial cortex are unique small, excitable pyramidal neurons that define the morphology of this brain region.
source_span: The small, excitable LR cells are unique among pyramidal cells in RSG, and there is no evidence, to our knowledge, for such cells in any other cortical regions... Thus, LR cells are the defining morphological feature of RSG.
selection_reasoning: This background fact situates the studied neurons anatomically and functionally, important for understanding the biological context.

fact: Low-rheobase (LR) neurons are a unique type of pyramidal cell found specifically in the granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) and are not present in other cortical regions.
source_span: excitable LR cells are unique among pyramidal cells in RSG , and there is no evidence , to our knowledge , for such cells in any other cortical regions
selection_reasoning: This background fact defines the cell type central to the study and its unique anatomical location, which is critical for understanding the research focus.

fact: LR neurons have distinct electrophysiological properties, including low rheobase and lack of spike frequency adaptation, which are their defining computational features.
source_span: the low rheobase and lack of spike frequency adaptation of these neurons are their defining computational features
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the key physiological characteristics that distinguish LR neurons and motivate their study.

fact: LR neurons play an integral role in the retrosplenial cortex's unique ability to process anterior thalamic head direction inputs.
source_span: The distinct electrophysiological properties of LR neurons , specifically , play an integral role in the RSG’s unique capacity to process anterior thalamic head direction inputs
selection_reasoning: This links the cell type to the main functional question of how spatial information is processed in the RSG.

fact: Thalamocortical synapses onto LR neurons exhibit synaptic depression.
source_span: We have shown that thalamocortical synapses onto LR cells are depressing
selection_reasoning: This synaptic property is a key mechanistic finding relevant to how LR neurons process input.

fact: Synaptic depression at thalamocortical synapses enables LR neurons to compute angular head speed from head direction input, resulting in robust encoding of angular speed in LR firing rates.
source_span: Our modeling results demonstrate that such depressing synapses allow LR neurons to compute angular head speed from head direction input , leading to robust encoding of angular speed in the postsynaptic LR firing rate
selection_reasoning: This principal finding connects synaptic physiology to a computational function central to the study.

fact: Anticipatory firing of head direction cells improves LR neurons' encoding of angular head speed by reducing time lag and strengthening correlation with head speed.
source_span: We also find that LR encoding of angular head speed is improved by the fact that input HD cells display anticipatory firing ... This improvement not only allows LR cells to encode current head speed with a shorter time lag , but also strengthens the correlation with head speed regardless of lag
selection_reasoning: This finding refines the understanding of how LR neurons achieve precise spatial coding.

fact: LR neurons receive spatial input from the dorsal subiculum, which transmits allocentric spatial information such as axis and boundary vector signals, targeting LR neurons predominantly in layer 3 of RSG.
source_span: The dorsal subiculum , which serves to transmit allocentric spatial information such as axis and boundary vector signals , also precisely targets LR neurons via projections predominantly to layer 3 of RSG
selection_reasoning: This fact describes a key anatomical input pathway relevant to the integration of spatial information by LR neurons.

fact: LR neurons integrate head direction input from the thalamus and spatial inputs from the hippocampal formation via the dorsal subiculum, supporting the retrosplenial cortex's role in processing directional and distance information.
source_span: Thus , the distinct morphology and intrinsic properties of LR neurons make them ideally suited to integrate head direction input from the thalamus and spatial inputs from the hippocampal formation via the dorsal subiculum ... this integration of various types of directional and distance information is often stated as the key computational function of the retrosplenial cortex as a whole
selection_reasoning: This summarizes the significance of LR neurons in the broader spatial processing function of the retrosplenial cortex.

fact: LR neurons can conjunctively encode both head direction and angular head speed at the level of individual cells.
source_span: we have shown that this thalamocortical synapse can support conjunctive encoding of both head direction and angular head speed by individual LR cells
selection_reasoning: This finding highlights the multiplexed coding capacity of LR neurons, a key functional insight.

fact: LR neurons in superficial RSG are predicted to show high firing rates and spike widths intermediate between regular-spiking and fast-spiking neurons, forming a distinct cluster identifiable in future in vivo recordings.
source_span: LR cells in superficial RSG are likely to show high firing rates and spike widths intermediate to the standard ‘broad/narrow’ criteria currently used to distinguish putative RS and FS cells in most cortical recordings ... future recordings will need a large sampling of cells in L2/3 of RSG to provide enough data to identify the predicted three distinct clusters of spike shapes ( RS/LR/FS )
selection_reasoning: This prediction about LR neuron firing properties is important for guiding future experimental validation.

fact: LR neuron activity is expected to correlate with angular head speed during behavior.
source_span: we expect LR cell activity to be correlated with angular head speed
selection_reasoning: This links the cellular findings to expected in vivo functional correlates, emphasizing translational relevance.

fact: LR cells in superficial retrosplenial granular cortex (RSG) are predicted to show high firing rates and spike widths intermediate between regular-spiking (RS) and fast-spiking (FS) cells.
source_span: First , based on their intrinsic properties ( Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Brennan et al . , 2020 ) , LR cells in superficial RSG are likely to show high firing rates and spike widths intermediate to the standard ‘broad/narrow’ criteria currently used to distinguish putative RS and FS cells in most cortical recordings .
selection_reasoning: This prediction about LR cell firing properties is a core background and mechanistic claim relevant to understanding their coding role.

fact: LR cell activity is expected to be correlated with angular head speed with a relatively small lag.
source_span: Second , we expect LR cell activity to be correlated with angular head speed with a relatively small lag ( Figures 8 and 9 ) .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal functional prediction about LR cells linking them to head movement encoding.

fact: The head velocity tuning curves of LR cells are predicted to be concave up and exhibit approximately quadratic scaling at low rotational speeds.
source_span: Third , we predict that the experimentally observed head velocity tuning curves will be concave up and exhibit approximately quadratic scaling at low rotational speeds , as our analytical work suggests ( Figure 8; Appendix ) .
selection_reasoning: This prediction about the shape of tuning curves is a key mechanistic insight into LR cell coding.

fact: A significant proportion of LR cells are predicted to show conjunctive encoding of both angular head speed and direction.
source_span: Fourth , we anticipate a significant proportion of LR cells will show conjunctive encoding , where both angular head speed and direction are encoded .
selection_reasoning: This conjunctive encoding is a central functional claim about LR cells' role in spatial orientation.

fact: Individual LR cells are predicted to show a tradeoff between directional and speed encoding, allowing the population to comprehensively encode conjunctive speed and directional information.
source_span: A key aspect of this conjunctive encoding , as predicted by our simulations ( Figure 10 ) , is that individual cells will show a tradeoff between directional and speed encoding . As a population , this is likely to allow LR cells to comprehensively encode conjunctive speed and directional information and provide this information to downstream targets , helping with spatial orientation computations within RSG .
selection_reasoning: This finding explains how LR cells collectively encode spatial information, a principal functional insight.

fact: LR neurons in RSG do not synapse onto neighboring excitatory neurons within layers 2/3 or layer 5 regular-spiking cells, indicating they likely do not provide substantial input to ipsilateral RS or LR cells.
source_span: LR neurons do not synapse onto neighboring excitatory neurons within layers 2/3 ( Brennan et al . , 2020 ) , and no ( 0/9 ) pairs tested in this study between LR and layer 5 RS cells exhibited connectivity ( data not shown ) . Thus , LR cells likely do not provide any substantial input to other LR cells or any RS cells located in layers 2–5 of ipsilateral RSG .
selection_reasoning: This connectivity finding is key to understanding LR cells' circuit role and output targets.

fact: LR neurons send their axons into the corpus callosum and likely target homotopic regions of contralateral RSG.
source_span: Instead , LR neurons send their axons into the corpus callosum and may likely target homotopic regions of contralateral RSG ( Brennan et al . , 2020; Kurotani et al . , 2013 ) .
selection_reasoning: This anatomical fact is important for understanding LR cells' role in interhemispheric communication.

fact: Inputs from contralateral RSG preferentially and strongly target RS neurons, with almost no recruitment of LR neurons.
source_span: Our supplementary results ( Figure 6—figure supplement 1 ) show that inputs from contralateral RSG preferentially and strongly target RS neurons , with almost no recruitment of LR neurons .
selection_reasoning: This finding clarifies the directionality and specificity of interhemispheric connectivity relevant to LR and RS cells.

fact: LR neurons in one hemisphere receive unilateral inputs from directional cells in the anterior thalamus, which they use to encode both speed and direction of head rotations.
source_span: Thus , we propose the following hypotheses for LR downstream targets and possible function: LR neurons in one hemisphere receive unilateral inputs from directional cells in the anterior thalamus ( Figures 1 , 2 and 6 ) . These inputs are utilized to encode information about both the speed and direction of head rotations ...
selection_reasoning: This is a core functional claim linking LR cells to thalamic inputs and spatial encoding.

fact: LR cells may serve to perform a hemispheric switch of rotational speed and direction information by transmitting this information to RS cells in contralateral RSG but not ipsilateral RSG.
source_span: and are subsequently transmitted to RS cells in contralateral , but not ipsilateral , RSG ( Figure 6—figure supplement 1 ) . Thus , LR cells may serve to perform a hemispheric switch of rotational speed and direction information .
selection_reasoning: This hypothesis about LR cells' role in interhemispheric information transfer is a principal implication.

fact: RS cells may use inputs from contralateral LR cells to compare actual head speed and direction signals with motor efference signals, helping to sharpen spatial orientation coding in RSG.
source_span: Given the known bidirectional connectivity between secondary motor cortex and RSG ( Yamawaki et al . , 2016a ) , RS cells may be able to utilize inputs from contralateral LR cells to perform comparisons of the actual head speed and direction signal with motor efference signals , helping to sharpen the code for spatial orientation in the RSG .
selection_reasoning: This functional implication links LR and RS cells to motor-sensory integration relevant to spatial orientation.

fact: Projections from the claustrum and anterior cingulate cortex avoid laminar overlap with LR apical dendrites and instead target RS apical and basal dendrites in lower layers.
source_span: In contrast to thalamic and DS inputs to RSG , projections from both the claustrum and anterior cingulate cortex avoid laminar overlap with LR apical dendrites , instead projecting to the lower divisions of L1/2 and L5 to target RS apical and basal dendrites ( Figures 3 and 4 , and 6 ) .
selection_reasoning: This anatomical fact distinguishes input pathways to LR versus RS cells, relevant to their functional specialization.

fact: The claustrum and anterior cingulate cortex are implicated in cognitive and mnemonic functions but also exhibit some degree of spatial information processing.
source_span: Both the CLA and ACC are heavily implicated in a range of non-spatial behaviors often described as being ‘cognitive’ or ‘mnemonic’ in function ... but there is also evidence that these regions exhibit some degree of spatial information processing ( Guterstam et al . , 2015; Jankowski and O'Mara , 2015; Sutherland et al . , 1988; Whishaw et al . , 2001 ) .
selection_reasoning: This background fact contextualizes the functional roles of CLA and ACC inputs to RS cells.

fact: The retrosplenial cortex (RSC) plays a key role in contextual fear conditioning by integrating spatial and non-spatial information.
source_span: This convergence of disparate signals onto RS cells could then serve to support functions that require both spatial and non-spatial integration, such as contextual fear conditioning, a key function attributed to the RSC (de Sousa et al., 2019; Keene and Bucci, 2008a; Keene and Bucci, 2008b; Kwapis et al., 2015; Yamawaki et al., 2019a).
selection_reasoning: This fact provides important background and significance about the functional role of the retrosplenial cortex relevant to the study's focus.

fact: Selective ablation of retrosplenial RS cells near the boundary and within upper layer 5 causes contextual fear amnesia, indicating these cells are involved in fear-related functions of the retrosplenial cortex.
source_span: Indeed, a recent study reported that selective ablation of putative retrosplenial RS cells located near the boundary and within upper layer 5 resulted in contextual fear amnesia (Sigwald et al., 2020), indicating that these cells are involved in the fear-related functions of the retrosplenial cortex (Lukoyanov and Lukoyanova, 2006; Yamawaki et al., 2019a; Yamawaki et al., 2019b).
selection_reasoning: This finding highlights a key causal link between specific retrosplenial neurons and fear conditioning, a principal finding relevant to the study.

fact: Retrosplenial RS neurons preferentially receive inputs from the claustrum (CLA) and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), which are brain regions implicated in fear-associated behaviors.
source_span: Both the CLA (Cho et al., 2017; Ipser et al., 2013; Vakolyuk et al., 1980; Vetere et al., 2017; Zingg et al., 2018) and ACC (Frankland et al., 2004; Han et al., 2003; Steenland et al., 2012) have been heavily implicated in fear-associated behaviors, suggesting again that CLA and ACC inputs to L3 RS cells help to support the role of these neurons in contextual fear conditioning.
selection_reasoning: This fact connects anatomical inputs to retrosplenial neurons with their functional role in fear, a key mechanistic insight.

fact: Layer 3 retrosplenial RS neurons receive direct spatial inputs from the claustrum and anterior cingulate cortex in addition to cognitive and mnemonic information.
source_span: Regardless, retrosplenial RS neurons may be receiving direct spatial inputs from the CLA and ACC in addition to the cognitive and mnemonic information relayed by these two regions.
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the nature of inputs to RS neurons, important for understanding the circuit basis of retrosplenial function.

fact: Retrosplenial LR neurons receive directional and spatial inputs from the anterior thalamus and dorsal subiculum.
source_span: LR neurons receive directional and spatial inputs from the anterior thalamus and dorsal subiculum.
selection_reasoning: This fact identifies a key input pathway to a specific retrosplenial neuron subtype, central to the study's main findings.

fact: Thalamic inputs to retrosplenial LR cells exhibit synaptic dynamics that can produce rate coding of angular head speed.
source_span: The synaptic dynamics of thalamic inputs to LR cells can give rise to rate coding of angular head speed in LR cells.
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights a principal functional mechanism discovered in the study.

fact: Neighboring retrosplenial RS neurons respond very weakly to directional inputs from the anterior thalamus and dorsal subiculum because their dendrites avoid overlap with these afferents.
source_span: In contrast, neighboring RS neurons in RSG respond very weakly to these directional inputs, as their apical and basal dendrites distinctly avoid laminar overlap with anterior thalamic and subicular afferents.
selection_reasoning: This fact contrasts the input specificity between neuron types, a key comparative finding.

fact: Feedforward inhibition regulates cortical signaling in retrosplenial circuits by modulating responses to thalamic and claustral inputs.
source_span: Matrix TC inputs evoke feedforward inhibition to regulate cortical signaling through both disinhibition (Anastasiades et al., 2021; Delevich et al., 2015) and the disynaptic inhibition of pyramidal neurons (Cruikshank et al., 2012; Yamawaki et al., 2019a; Yamawaki et al., 2019b). Similarly, ClaC inputs invoke feedforward inhibition in several cortical regions, particularly through recruitment of neuropeptide Y (NPY) and, to a lesser degree, FS cells (Jackson et al., 2018).
selection_reasoning: This fact provides important mechanistic context about inhibitory regulation in the retrosplenial circuit.

fact: Long-range inhibitory signals from hippocampal CA1 target apical dendrites in retrosplenial layer 1a, converging with excitatory anterior thalamic inputs to regulate retrosplenial network activity.
source_span: Long-range inhibitory signals from CA1 of the hippocampus also target apical dendrites in retrosplenial layer 1a, converging with excitatory anterior thalamic inputs, to precisely regulate these TC inputs and establish a hippocampo-thalamo-retrosplenial network (Yamawaki et al., 2019b).
selection_reasoning: This fact describes a key circuit interaction relevant to retrosplenial information processing.

fact: The study used a mouse model circuit consisting of retrosplenial LR cells receiving input from thalamic head direction cells with synapses exhibiting short-term depression.
source_span: Our model circuit consists of an RSG LR cell receiving input from an ensemble of N thalamic HD cells, via synapses exhibiting short-term depression.
selection_reasoning: This fact summarizes a key methodological approach relevant to the main findings.

fact: Thalamic head direction cells exhibit an anticipatory time interval (ATI), firing before the animal's head reaches the cell's preferred direction.
source_span: Thalamic HD cells exhibit an anticipatory time interval, or ATI: for each cell, there exists some constant duration Ams such that the cell tends to spike Ams prior to when the animal’s heading equals the preferred direction of the cell.
selection_reasoning: This fact defines an important property of the input neurons modeled, relevant to understanding the circuit function.

fact: Head direction (HD) cell preferred angles shift in anticipation of angular head velocity, effectively transforming the perceived heading trajectory.
source_span: The ATI is defined via the property that when angular head velocity equals ω , the PA of this cell shifts from θ to θ-ωA . Equivalently , we can think of HD cell PAs as static and instead say anticipatory firing effectively transforms the heading trajectory itself: if θTt describes the true angular trajectory , the effective trajectory experienced by our chosen HD cell is:θA ( t ) =θT ( t ) +A⋅θT˙ ( t )
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the core concept of anticipatory firing in HD cells, which is central to the study's background and modeling approach.

fact: In vivo mouse head tracking recordings were used to simulate angular head trajectories for studying HD cell activity.
source_span: To simulate the angular trajectory θTt , we employ in vivo mouse head tracking recordings from the data set CRCNS-th1 ( Peyrache et al . , 2015 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the key data source and biological system used to model head direction signals.

fact: The Tsodyks-Markram (TM) model of short-term synaptic plasticity was used to characterize synaptic dynamics at HD cell inputs.
source_span: In the Tsodyks-Markram ( TM ) model ( Tsodyks et al . , 1998 ) of short-term synaptic plasticity , each synapse has a finite pool from which it releases vesicles into the cleft upon arrival of a presynaptic spike .
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the main synaptic plasticity model applied to understand synaptic behavior in the study.

fact: Synaptic depression and facilitation dynamics depend on the relative timescales of depression recovery and facilitation decay in the TM model.
source_span: In the regime of τd≫τf , depression dominates the synaptic dynamics; conversely , in the regime of τf≫τd , facilitation dominates . Accordingly , the limits τf→0 and τd→0 describe depression-only and facilitation-only dynamics , respectively .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the key mechanism of synaptic plasticity dynamics relevant to the study's modeling.

fact: Parameters for the TM model were fitted to experimental EPSP data from thalamocortical stimulation of retrosplenial granular (RSG) low-rheobase (LR) cells, resulting in moderately depressing synaptic dynamics.
source_span: We obtained this parameter set by fitting the TM model response to recorded EPSP amplitudes evoked via thalamocortical stimulation of RSG LR cells with a 10 Hz pulse train ... The resultant TM dynamics were moderately depressing , in accordance with the experimental results .
selection_reasoning: This fact links the model parameters to experimental data, supporting the biological relevance of the simulations.

fact: The postsynaptic LR cell was modeled using a morphologically detailed Hodgkin-Huxley conductance-based model including fast sodium, delayed rectifier potassium, and Kv1.1-mediated slow potassium currents.
source_span: We model the postsynaptic LR cell using the morphologically detailed model originally presented in Brennan et al . , 2020 . This model , implemented in NEURON ... consists of Hodgkin-Huxley conductances representing a fast sodium current , a delayed rectifier potassium current , and a Kv1 . 1-mediated slow potassium current .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the key postsynaptic neuron model used to study synaptic input integration.

fact: Each postsynaptic LR cell receives input from multiple presynaptic HD cells, each with a unique preferred angle (PA).
source_span: Each postsynaptic cell receives input from N presynaptic HD cells , each of which has a unique PA .
selection_reasoning: This fact is central to the network input structure and the study of how HD inputs shape postsynaptic responses.

fact: Preferred angle distributions of presynaptic HD cells were modeled both as uniform random and as nonuniform continuous distributions generated by Brownian bridge processes.
source_span: When studying postsynaptic speed coding , we initially drew the PA of each HD cell uniformly at random from 0 , 2π . Later on , we examined the effect of introducing nonuniform PA distributions ... modeled the PA distribution probability densities randomly as resulting from Brownian bridge processes ( to ensure 2π periodicity of the density ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes a key methodological variation to study the effect of input tuning on postsynaptic coding.

fact: Postsynaptic activity reflecting head turning speed was quantified using time-lagged Pearson correlation and mutual information between firing rate and head turning speed.
source_span: To quantify the extent to which postsynaptic activity reflects head turning speed , we utilized two similarity measures M: Pearson correlation and mutual information . In fact , we used the time-lagged counterparts of these measures ...
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the main analytical approach to assess the relationship between neural activity and behavior.

fact: Petal number is invariant in Arabidopsis thaliana flowers but varies in the closely related species Cardamine hirsuta.
source_span: Petal number, for example, is invariant in Arabidopsis thaliana flowers. However, petal number varies in the closely related species Cardamine hirsuta, and the genetic basis for this difference between species is unknown.
selection_reasoning: This fact establishes the key biological difference motivating the study and frames the main research question.

fact: Divergence in the floral regulator APETALA1 (AP1) explains the species-specific difference in petal number robustness between Arabidopsis thaliana and Cardamine hirsuta.
source_span: Here we show that divergence in the pleiotropic floral regulator APETALA1 (AP1) can account for the species-specific difference in petal number robustness.
selection_reasoning: This is the principal finding linking a specific gene to the difference in petal number robustness, central to the study's claim.

fact: Arabidopsis thaliana AP1 confers robustness in petal number by masking the effects of quantitative trait loci controlling petal number in Cardamine hirsuta.
source_span: This large effect of AP1 is explained by epistatic interactions: A. thaliana AP1 confers robustness by masking the phenotypic expression of quantitative trait loci controlling petal number in C. hirsuta.
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the mechanism by which AP1 affects petal number robustness, a key insight into genetic interactions.

fact: Cardamine hirsuta AP1 fails to complement the robustness function of Arabidopsis thaliana AP1, resulting in variable petal number.
source_span: We show that C. hirsuta AP1 fails to complement this function of A. thaliana AP1, conferring variable petal number, and that upstream regulatory regions of AP1 contribute to this divergence.
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the functional divergence of AP1 between species, explaining the phenotypic difference.

fact: Upstream regulatory regions of AP1 contribute to the divergence in petal number robustness between Arabidopsis thaliana and Cardamine hirsuta.
source_span: …and that upstream regulatory regions of AP1 contribute to this divergence.
selection_reasoning: This identifies a genetic basis for the functional differences in AP1, important for understanding evolutionary changes.

fact: Variable petal number is maintained in Cardamine hirsuta despite sufficient genetic variation in natural populations to produce four-petalled flowers.
source_span: Moreover, variable petal number is maintained in C. hirsuta despite sufficient standing genetic variation in natural accessions to produce plants with four-petalled flowers.
selection_reasoning: This fact shows that genetic variation alone does not fix petal number, indicating evolutionary or regulatory factors maintain variability.

fact: Petal number is a robust trait in flowering plants, usually invariant within species and higher taxonomic orders, likely due to stabilizing selection.
source_span: Petal number is a robust trait in flowering plants and usually invariant within species and even higher taxonomic orders… suggesting that this trait was canalized during angiosperm evolution to produce a stable phenotype in the face of genetic and environmental perturbation.
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains why petal number robustness is biologically important and evolutionarily conserved.

fact: A stable number of petals helps ensure reliable flower opening and pollinator attraction, supporting reproductive success.

fact: Cardamine hirsuta flowers display variable petal number ranging from zero to four petals on a single plant, influenced by environmental and genetic factors.

fact: Environmental factors such as day length, winter cold, and ambient temperature influence petal number in Cardamine hirsuta flowers.

fact: Understanding the genetic basis of developmental traits and their evolution is a major goal of evolutionary developmental biology.

fact: Petal number is a robust phenotype in Arabidopsis thaliana, with flowers consistently producing four petals across genetically diverse accessions.
source_span: The flowers of A . thaliana and other Brassicaceae species are readily distinguished by their four petals . This phenotype is robust to natural genetic variation; for example , flowers from genetically diverse A . thaliana accessions consistently produce four petals

fact: The Cardamine hirsuta AP1 gene fails to complement the petal number robustness function of Arabidopsis thaliana AP1, resulting in variable petal number.

fact: Differences in upstream regulatory regions of the AP1 gene contribute to the divergence in petal number robustness between Arabidopsis thaliana and Cardamine hirsuta.

fact: Previous methods for purifying intestinal cells in planarians include magnetic bead feeding and single-cell profiling, but these have limitations such as confounding effects of feeding and low intestinal cell abundance.
source_span: Previously , we developed a method for purifying intestinal phagocytes from single-cell suspensions derived from planarians fed magnetic beads , enabling characterization of gene expression by this cell type ( Forsthoefel et al . , 2012 ) . More recently , single-cell profiling of whole planarians has distinguished individual intestinal cell types , as well as transitional markers for neoblasts differentiating along endodermal lineages ( Fincher et al . , 2018; Labbé et al . , 2012; Zeng et al . , 2018; Plass et al . , 2018 ) . Both approaches have advanced our understanding of intestinal biology . However , methods that ( a ) avoid the potentially confounding effects of feeding and dissociation on gene expression and ( b ) overcome the need to sequence tens of thousands of planarian cells to identify intestinal cells ( only 1–3% of all planarian cells , [Baguñá and Romero , 1981] ) , would further enhance the experimental accessibility of the intestine .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the limitations of existing methods and the need for improved approaches.

fact: Laser-capture microdissection (LCM) is a precise method for obtaining enriched or pure cell populations from tissue samples and has been applied to planarian intestine for expression profiling.
source_span: Laser-capture microdissection ( LCM ) was developed as a precise method for obtaining enriched or pure cell populations from tissue samples , including archived biopsy and surgical specimens ( Emmert-Buck et al . , 1996 ) . ... Here , we report the application of LCM for expression profiling of the planarian intestine .
