selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the biological importance of mitochondrial protein quality control.

fact: In yeast, mitophagy primarily functions to adapt to metabolic changes rather than in protein quality control.
source_span: In yeast , however , mitophagy appears to function primarily to adapt to metabolic changes , rather than in protein QC ( Fukuda and Kanki , 2018; Kanki et al . , 2015 ) .
selection_reasoning: This clarifies why mitophagy is not the main pathway for mitochondrial protein quality control in yeast.

fact: There is little evidence that mitophagy in yeast is ubiquitin-dependent, consistent with the absence of yeast orthologues of Parkin or PINK1.
source_span: Furthermore , there is little evidence indicating that mitophagy is ubiquitin-dependent , in accordance with the absence of obvious yeast orthologues of Parkin or PINK1 ( Belgareh-Touzé et al . , 2017; Tan et al . , 2016 ) .
selection_reasoning: This supports the rationale for studying alternative ubiquitin-dependent mitochondrial quality control pathways in yeast.

fact: The mitochondrial outer membrane is fully accessible to cytosolic proteasomes, enabling ubiquitin-proteasome system-mediated degradation of outer membrane proteins.
source_span: While there is no evidence for proteasomes inside mitochondria , the mitochondrial outer membrane ( MOM ) is fully accessible to cytosolic proteasomes .
selection_reasoning: This fact underpins the feasibility of ubiquitin-proteasome degradation of mitochondrial outer membrane proteins.

fact: The study reveals a unique quality control pathway for misfolded mitochondrial outer membrane proteins that involves both cytosolic and mitochondrial factors and is distinct from other cellular quality control pathways.
source_span: This study reveals a unique QC pathway comprised of a combination of cytosolic and mitochondrial factors that distinguish it from other cellular QC pathways .
selection_reasoning: This summarizes the significance and novelty of the findings.

fact: The regulated recognition and ubiquitination of the mitofusin Fzo1 by the SCFMdm30 E3 ligase and its subsequent proteasomal degradation are integral to mitochondrial outer membrane (MOM) fusion.
source_span: The regulated recognition and ubiquitination of this mitofusin by SCFMdm30 ( Skp1-Cullin-F-box E3 with F-box protein Mdm30 ) and its subsequent proteasomal degradation are integral to the process of MOM fusion ( Cohen et al . , 2011; Cohen et al . , 2008; Escobar-Henriques et al . , 2006 ) .
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains a key known mechanism of MOM protein regulation relevant to the study of mitochondrial protein quality control.

fact: The AAA-ATPase Msp1 is required for extraction of mislocalized tail-anchored proteins from the mitochondrial outer membrane prior to their degradation by ER-associated degradation (ERAD) machinery.
source_span: The degradation of tail-anchored proteins mislocalized to the MOM uniquely requires the AAA-ATPase Msp1 for extraction from the MOM prior to transfer to the ER where they are degraded by ERAD machinery ( Matsumoto et al . , 2019; Okreglak and Walter , 2014; Wohlever et al . , 2017 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact provides important context about known mitochondrial protein quality control pathways relevant to the study.

fact: A universal mitochondrial-associated degradation (MAD) pathway for mitochondrial outer membrane proteins has not been described, and many steps in substrate degradation remain unexamined.
source_span: Thus , a universal MAD pathway for MOM proteins has not been described and many steps in substrate degradation remain unexamined .
selection_reasoning: This highlights the knowledge gap motivating the study.

fact: Temperature-sensitive peripheral mitochondrial outer membrane proteins sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts were established as quality control substrates to study mitochondrial degradation.
source_span: In this study , we establish temperature-sensitive ( ts- ) peripheral MOM proteins ( sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts ) as QC substrates .
selection_reasoning: This describes the key experimental model used to investigate mitochondrial protein quality control.

fact: The temperature-sensitive nature of sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts, combined with their tight association with the mitochondrial outer membrane, enables study of their mitochondrial degradation without concerns of mislocalization.
source_span: The ts- nature of these substrates , coupled with their tight association with the MOM , enabled study of their mitochondrial degradation without concerns of mislocalization to the cytosol or elsewhere .
selection_reasoning: This explains why these substrates are suitable models for studying mitochondrial degradation.

fact: Proteasomal degradation of these mitochondrial-associated degradation (MAD) quality control substrates occurs at the mitochondrial outer membrane and requires specific cytosolic and mitochondrial ubiquitin-proteasome system components conserved in higher eukaryotes.
source_span: The proteasomal degradation of these MAD QC substrates occurs at the MOM and requires specific cytosolic and mitochondrial UPS components , most of which are conserved in higher eukaryotes .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding about the mechanism and conservation of the degradation pathway.

fact: The study reveals a requirement for factors not previously implicated in the degradation of native mitochondrial-associated degradation substrates, defining a distinct quality control pathway.
source_span: Our results reveal a requirement for factors not previously implicated in the degradation of native MAD substrates and the combination of components identified defines a distinct QC pathway .
selection_reasoning: This highlights the novelty and significance of the findings.

fact: Sam35 is an essential mitochondrial outer membrane protein that acts as the substrate receptor of the sorting and assembly machinery (SAM) complex required for assembly of β-barrel proteins into the mitochondrial outer membrane.
source_span: Sam35 is the substrate receptor of the MOM-embedded multiprotein sorting and assembly machinery ( SAM ) complex required for assembly of β-barrel proteins into the MOM ( Chan and Lithgow , 2008; Kozjak et al . , 2003; Kutik et al . , 2008; Milenkovic et al . , 2004 ) .
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the biological role of one of the key proteins studied.

fact: Sen2 is an essential mitochondrial outer membrane protein that provides endonuclease activity for the tRNA splicing endonuclease complex and cleaves mitochondria-targeted non-stop mRNA.
source_span: Sen2 provides endonuclease activity for the multi-subunit tRNA splicing endonuclease complex and also cleaves a mitochondria-targeted non-stop mRNA ( Ho et al . , 1990; Tsuboi et al . , 2015; Winey and Culbertson , 1988 ) .
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the biological role of the other key protein studied.

fact: The temperature-sensitive alleles sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts encode full-length proteins containing multiple missense mutations that likely cause their temperature-sensitive phenotypes.
source_span: We first determined that sam35-2ts and sen2-1ts encoded full-length proteins . Each contained multiple missense mutations ( Figure 1—figure supplement 1A ) that likely account for the phenotypes reported ( Li et al . , 2011; Milenkovic et al . , 2004; Winey and Culbertson , 1988 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact supports the validity of the model substrates used to study protein misfolding and degradation.

fact: Genome-integrated sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts support cell viability at the permissive temperature (25°C) but not at the non-permissive temperature (37°C), consistent with their temperature-sensitive nature.
source_span: Genome-integrated versions of sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts support cell viability at the permissive ( 25°C ) but not non-permissive temperature ( 37°C; Figure 1A ) , consistent with the previously-described untagged versions ( Li et al . , 2011; Milenkovic et al . , 2004; Winey and Culbertson , 1988 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact confirms the temperature-sensitive phenotype relevant to the study of protein quality control.

fact: Increasing the temperature to 37°C results in dramatic destabilization of sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts proteins relative to wild-type proteins, indicating misfolding-induced instability.
source_span: We find that increasing the temperature to 37°C results in dramatic destabilization of the ts- proteins relative to the WT proteins ( Figure 1B ) .
selection_reasoning: This finding demonstrates that the temperature-sensitive alleles undergo misfolding leading to degradation.

fact: The temperature-sensitive sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts proteins remain localized to the mitochondrial outer membrane after temperature-induced destabilization.
source_span: Co-expression of sam35-2GFPts and sen2-1GFPts with a mitochondrial marker ( mtRFP ) demonstrated that the ts- proteins remain mitochondrial after the temperature increase ( Figure 1C ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact validates that degradation occurs at the mitochondria rather than due to mislocalization.

fact: Subcellular fractionation confirmed that sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts proteins fractionate almost exclusively to the mitochondrial pellet at 37°C despite their destabilization.
source_span: Consistent with our microscopy , sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts fractionated almost exclusively to the mitochondrial pellet at 37°C ( P; Figure 1D ) .
selection_reasoning: This supports the conclusion that these proteins remain mitochondrial during degradation.

fact: sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts are temperature-sensitive mitochondrial outer membrane proteins that remain localized to mitochondria even when destabilized at non-permissive temperatures.
source_span: Consistent with our microscopy , sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts fractionated almost exclusively to the mitochondrial pellet at 37°C ( P; Figure 1D ) . A similar fractionation pattern was observed with chromosomal HA-tagged ts- alleles ( Figure 1—figure supplement 1F ) . Therefore , sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts are destabilized at the non-permissive temperature yet remain mitochondrially-localized , validating their use as model MAD QC substrates .
selection_reasoning: This establishes the model substrates and their mitochondrial localization, which is essential background and motivation for studying mitochondrial-associated degradation (MAD).

fact: The degradation of sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts at non-permissive temperature depends on proteasome function but not on vacuolar or mitochondrial resident proteases.
source_span: The turnover of sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts was assessed at the non-permissive temperature in strains containing conditional mutations in the 20S core ( pre1-1 pre2-2; Figure 2A ) or the 19S cap ( cim3-1; Figure 2B ) of the 26S proteasome . Both ts- proteins were substantially stabilized in these mutants relative to isogenic WT strains . In contrast , vacuolar or mitochondrial resident proteases were not required for sam35-2HAts or sen2-1HAts turnover ( Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B ) .
selection_reasoning: This identifies the proteasome as the key degradation machinery for these mitochondrial outer membrane substrates, a principal mechanistic finding.

fact: sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts accumulate at mitochondria when proteasome function is impaired, indicating their degradation occurs at the mitochondrial outer membrane.
source_span: Thus , these data indicate that sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts primarily accumulate at the mitochondria when their proteasomal degradation is blocked .
selection_reasoning: This supports the conclusion that degradation occurs at mitochondria rather than elsewhere, clarifying the site of quality control.

fact: Ubiquitination is required for the degradation of sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts, as shown by their stabilization in a ubiquitin-activating enzyme mutant and accumulation of ubiquitinated forms when proteasome function is inhibited.
source_span: Consistent with being UPS substrates , stabilization of both sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts was observed in a ts- mutant of the ubiquitin-activating enzyme ( uba1-204; Figure 2D; Ghaboosi and Deshaies , 2007 ) , indicating that ubiquitination is required for their degradation . Moreover , ubiquitin-modified forms of sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts were evident when proteasome function was inhibited ( Figure 2E and F and see Figure 2—figure supplement 1F for an additional control ) , as indicated by characteristic higher molecular weight bands and a smear representing highly ubiquitinated species ( Emmerich and Cohen , 2015 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact establishes the involvement of the ubiquitin-proteasome system in the turnover of these mitochondrial proteins, a key mechanistic insight.

fact: The known mitochondrial ubiquitin ligases Mdm30 and Rsp5 do not affect the stability of sam35-2HAts or sen2-1HAts, indicating other E3 ligases mediate their degradation.
source_span: We assessed whether these E3s also play a role in MAD of QC substrates and found that strains lacking either Mdm30 or Rsp5 function did not affect sam35-2HAts or sen2-1HAts stability ( Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B ) .
selection_reasoning: This narrows down the responsible ubiquitin ligases, motivating the search for other E3s involved in mitochondrial quality control.

fact: The E3 ubiquitin ligase San1 is required for efficient degradation of sam35-2HAts, while the E3 ligase Ubr1 is required for efficient degradation of sen2-1HAts.
source_span: Interestingly , we found that san1Δ impaired turnover of sam35-2HAts ( Figure 3A , middle panel ) , while ubr1Δ impaired turnover of sen2-1HAts ( Figure 3B , middle panel ) .
selection_reasoning: Identifying specific E3 ligases responsible for targeting these substrates is a principal finding that advances understanding of mitochondrial protein quality control.

fact: Deletion of both San1 and Ubr1 leads to greater stabilization of sam35-2HAts than deletion of San1 alone, indicating that Ubr1 can partially compensate for loss of San1 in targeting sam35-2HAts.
source_span: While ubr1Δ alone did not affect sam35-2HAts turnover ( Figure 3—figure supplement 1C ) , loss of Ubr1 in conjunction with san1Δ led to greater stabilization than loss of San1 alone ( Figure 3A , lower panel ) , indicating that Ubr1 can target sam35-2HAts in the absence of San1 .
selection_reasoning: This reveals functional redundancy or cooperation between E3 ligases in mitochondrial protein quality control.

fact: Polyubiquitination of sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts is greatly reduced when San1 or Ubr1, respectively, are deleted, confirming their roles in substrate ubiquitination.
source_span: Notably , the polyubiquitination of sam35-2HAts ( Figure 3C ) and sen2-1HAts ( Figure 3D ) was greatly reduced when San1 or Ubr1 , respectively , were deleted .
selection_reasoning: This provides biochemical evidence that these E3 ligases directly mediate ubiquitination of the substrates.

fact: Loss of the E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme Ubc4 stabilizes sen2-1HAts to a similar degree as loss of Ubr1, indicating Ubc4 functions with Ubr1 in sen2-1HAts degradation.
source_span: Loss of Ubc4 , an E2 known to function with Ubr1 for select substrates , stabilized sen2-1HAts to a similar degree as ubr1Δ ( Figure 3E ) .
selection_reasoning: This identifies the E2 enzyme cooperating with Ubr1, clarifying the ubiquitination machinery involved.

fact: Both sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts remain localized to mitochondria in strains lacking San1 or Ubr1, respectively, confirming that these E3 ligases act on substrates at the mitochondrial outer membrane.
source_span: To confirm that Ubr1 and San1 can act on ts- proteins at the MOM , we examined the localization of sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts by fractionation in san1Δ and ubr1Δ , respectively . In these strains , both ts- proteins still accumulated almost exclusively in the pellet fraction
selection_reasoning: This supports the conclusion that the identified E3 ligases function at mitochondria, reinforcing the mitochondrial quality control context.

fact: The E3 ubiquitin ligases San1 and Ubr1 function as components of the mitochondrial-associated degradation (MAD) machinery for proteasome-mediated degradation of mitochondrial outer membrane temperature-sensitive proteins sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts.
source_span: These results establish that San1 and Ubr1 can function as components of the MAD machinery for proteasome-mediated degradation of sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts, respectively.
selection_reasoning: This identifies key enzymes responsible for degrading mitochondrial quality control substrates, a principal finding central to the study.

fact: The cytosolic SSA family of Hsp70 chaperones is required for the degradation of mitochondrial temperature-sensitive proteins sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts, as their inactivation strongly stabilizes these proteins.
source_span: Interestingly, both sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts were strongly stabilized in a conditional yeast strain where three SSA family members are deleted and the fourth (SSA1) is ts- (ssa1-45ts; ssa1-45ts ssa2Δ ssa3Δ ssa4Δ) relative to the control strain (SSA1; SSA1 ssa2Δ ssa3Δ ssa4Δ; Figure 4A).
selection_reasoning: This shows the importance of Hsp70 chaperones in mitochondrial protein quality control, a key mechanistic insight.

fact: SSA1 Hsp70 chaperone is required for ubiquitination of mitochondrial temperature-sensitive proteins sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts, as ubiquitin-modified forms are dramatically reduced when SSA1 is inactivated.
source_span: Notably, the SSA1 chaperone was also required for ubiquitination: despite the accumulation of unmodified sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts, ubiquitin-modified forms are dramatically reduced when SSA1 is inactivated (Figure 4C).
selection_reasoning: This links chaperone function to the ubiquitination step, a key mechanism in protein degradation.

fact: Degradation of native mitochondrial outer membrane UPS substrate Fzo1HA is largely unaffected by loss of SSA Hsp70 chaperone function, indicating different chaperone requirements for native versus non-native MAD substrates.
source_span: In contrast to the ts- proteins, degradation of the native MOM UPS substrate, Fzo1HA, was largely unaffected by loss SSA function (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
selection_reasoning: This highlights a significant distinction in chaperone dependency between substrate types, relevant for understanding MAD specificity.

fact: Hsp40 co-chaperone Sis1 is required for efficient degradation of mitochondrial temperature-sensitive proteins sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts, while the Hsp40 co-chaperone Ydj1 is not.
source_span: Depletion of ~90% of Sis1 protein using Sis1 DAmP cells slowed the turnover of both sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts, while loss of Ydj1 or its ortholog, Hlj1, did not.
selection_reasoning: This identifies specific co-chaperones involved in mitochondrial protein quality control, refining the chaperone network.

fact: The degradation of mitochondrial quality control substrates sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts depends on Hsp70 and Hsp40 chaperones but is independent of nuclear import factors such as Sse1, Hsc82/Hsp82, Sti1, Hsp104, and Dsk2.
source_span: These results establish that the degradation of the mitochondrial QC substrates is dependent on both Hsp70 and Hsp40 chaperones, but independent of nuclear import.
selection_reasoning: This clarifies the cellular localization and pathway specificity of mitochondrial protein degradation.

fact: The AAA-ATPase Cdc48 and its cofactors Npl4 and Ufd1 are required for efficient proteasomal degradation of mitochondrial quality control substrates sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts.
source_span: Both sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts were stabilized in conditional Cdc48, Npl4, and Ufd1 strains.
selection_reasoning: This identifies a critical ATPase complex involved in mitochondrial protein degradation, a principal mechanistic finding.

fact: Loss of the mitochondrial AAA-ATPase Msp1 does not stabilize mitochondrial temperature-sensitive proteins sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts, indicating Msp1 is not involved in their degradation.
source_span: In contrast, loss of Msp1, another AAA-ATPase that localizes to mitochondria and dislocates mislocalized tail-anchored proteins from the MOM, stabilized neither sam35-2HAts nor sen2-1HAts.
selection_reasoning: This distinguishes the role of different AAA-ATPases in mitochondrial protein quality control.

fact: In the absence of a functional Cdc48-Npl4-Ufd1 complex, ubiquitinated mitochondrial quality control substrates sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts accumulate and largely retain their mitochondrial localization.
source_span: Accordingly, we detected a relative increase in ubiquitinated sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts in Cdc48-Npl4-Ufd1 complex mutants... both substrates remain primarily mitochondrial.
selection_reasoning: This shows the role of the Cdc48 complex downstream of ubiquitination and its importance for substrate processing.

fact: Proteasome shuttling factors Rad23, Dsk2, and Ddi1 are not required for the degradation of mitochondrial quality control substrates sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts, distinguishing mitochondrial-associated degradation (MAD) from ER-associated degradation (ERAD).
source_span: Deletion of these or another proteasome shuttling factor, Ddi1, did not affect the degradation of sam35-2HAts or sen2-1HAts, further distinguishing MAD from ERAD.
selection_reasoning: This highlights mechanistic differences between mitochondrial and ER protein quality control pathways.

fact: Ubiquitinated mitochondrial quality control substrates require the Cdc48-Npl4-Ufd1 complex for efficient proteasomal degradation.
source_span: All together, these results indicate that ubiquitinated mitochondrial QC substrates require the Cdc48-Npl4-Ufd1 complex for efficient proteasomal degradation.
selection_reasoning: This is a core mechanistic finding about mitochondrial protein degradation central to the study.

fact: Loss of the Cdc48 co-factor Ubx2 significantly stabilizes mitochondrial temperature-sensitive proteins sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts, indicating its role in their degradation.
source_span: Notably, only the loss of Ubx2 significantly stabilized sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts.
selection_reasoning: Identifies a key co-factor involved in mitochondrial protein quality control, a principal finding.

fact: Ubx2 physically associates with mitochondrial temperature-sensitive proteins and their ubiquitinated forms accumulate in the absence of Ubx2.
source_span: We also detected a physical association between Ubx2-FLAG and the ts- proteins as assessed by co-immunoprecipitation... ubiquitinated forms of the ts- substrates accumulated in the absence of Ubx2.
selection_reasoning: Supports the mechanism by which Ubx2 facilitates degradation, important for understanding the pathway.

fact: Ubx2 localizes to both the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria, as confirmed by microscopy and biochemical fractionation.
source_span: We also confirmed this by co-localization of Ubx2-GFP with both ER (Sec63-RFP) and mitochondrial (mtRFP) markers by microscopy... The mitochondrial localization of a portion of Ubx2 was further verified biochemically by isolation of mitochondria.
selection_reasoning: Provides important background on the localization of a key protein involved in mitochondrial protein degradation.

fact: Degradation of mitochondrial temperature-sensitive proteins sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts is independent of ER-mitochondrial contact sites and ER-associated degradation machinery.
source_span: The turnover of sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts was unaffected in strains mutant for each of the four ERMES components... ts- protein degradation is unaffected by combined loss of the major ERAD E2s, Ubc6 and Ubc7, or E3s, Doa10 and Hrd1.
selection_reasoning: Clarifies that mitochondrial protein degradation occurs independently of ER pathways, a key conclusion.

fact: Degradation of mitochondrial temperature-sensitive proteins sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts is independent of the mitochondrial extraction factor Msp1.
source_span: Degradation of sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts is independent of Msp1.
selection_reasoning: Distinguishes the studied degradation pathway from other known mitochondrial quality control mechanisms.

fact: Ubx2 and, to a lesser extent, Doa1 stabilize the native mitochondrial outer membrane protein Fzo1HA by facilitating its ubiquitin-proteasome system-dependent degradation.
source_span: We find that loss of Ubx2 and, to a lesser extent, Doa1, stabilizes Fzo1HA, which is a native MOM UPS substrate... we also establish that Fzo1HA physically interacts with Ubx2, accompanied by an increase in ubiquitinated forms.
selection_reasoning: Extends the significance of Ubx2 to native mitochondrial protein turnover, highlighting its broader role.

fact: The mitochondrial temperature-sensitive proteins sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts accumulate predominantly in the mitochondrial fraction during proteasome impairment or Ubx2 loss, indicating their degradation occurs at mitochondria.
source_span: Fractionation data in the proteasome mutant strain... strongly suggests that ts- protein degradation occurs from the mitochondria. Sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts also largely accumulate in the mitochondrial pellet in ubx2Δ cells.
selection_reasoning: Supports the conclusion that degradation occurs at mitochondria rather than ER, important for understanding the pathway location.

fact: Mitochondria are essential to cellular bioenergetics and metabolism, making quality control mechanisms that dispose of damaged mitochondrial proteins vital for cellular function.
source_span: Mitochondria are essential to cellular bioenergetics and metabolism . It is therefore vital that QC mechanisms dispose of damaged proteins that can compromise function .
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the biological importance and motivation for studying mitochondrial protein quality control.

fact: In mammalian cells, damaged mitochondria are removed at the macroscopic level through mitophagy.
source_span: In mammalian cells , this is accomplished at the macroscopic level through mitophagy ( Pickles et al . , 2018 ) .
selection_reasoning: This provides context on existing mitochondrial quality control mechanisms in higher organisms, highlighting the need to study other pathways.

fact: This study defines a ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS)-mediated pathway for degradation of individual dysfunctional yeast mitochondrial outer membrane (MOM) proteins using two newly established model quality control substrates, sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts.
source_span: Here , we define a UPS-mediated pathway for the degradation of individual dysfunctional yeast MOM proteins using two newly-established model QC substrates , sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts ( schematized in Figure 7 ) .
selection_reasoning: This states the main research question and the novel model substrates used to study mitochondrial protein degradation.

fact: The sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts substrates contain mutations that render them unstable at non-permissive temperatures, mimicking damaged or misfolded proteins.
source_span: While previous mitochondrial UPS substrates have consisted primarily of native proteins ... sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts contain mutations that render them unstable at the non-permissive temperature , and thus mimic damaged , misfolded proteins .
selection_reasoning: This explains the rationale for using these model substrates to study mitochondrial protein quality control.

fact: The mitochondrial-associated degradation (MAD) quality control pathway characterized here requires both cytosolic and mitochondrial machinery and is distinct from other cellular quality control pathways.
source_span: These new mitochondrial model substrates have revealed a tightly-coupled degradation pathway at the MOM that requires both cytosolic and mitochondrial machinery . This MAD QC pathway ... is also not identical to any other cellular QC pathway , although there are points of intersection .
selection_reasoning: This highlights the novelty and distinctiveness of the identified degradation pathway.

fact: All mitochondrial protein degradation pathways described require 26S proteasome activity.
source_span: All of these degradation pathways , unsurprisingly , require 26S proteasome activity .
selection_reasoning: This fact is central to understanding the mechanism of protein degradation in mitochondria.

fact: The AAA-ATPase complex Cdc48-Npl4-Ufd1 is involved in mitochondrial protein degradation pathways, but the AAA-ATPase Msp1 is dispensable for degradation of mitochondrial temperature-sensitive substrates.
source_span: In many cases , the involvement of the Cdc48-Npl4-Ufd1 AAA-ATPase complex represents another point of convergence ... We found Msp1 to be dispensable for the degradation of mitochondrial ts- substrates .
selection_reasoning: This distinguishes the roles of different AAA-ATPases in mitochondrial protein quality control.

fact: The MAD quality control pathway characterized here is distinct from the pathway involving Msp1-dependent extraction and ER re-targeting of mislocalized tail-anchored proteins, as ts- substrates remain mitochondrial and are degraded independently of ER-associated degradation (ERAD) E2s or E3s.
source_span: The MAD QC pathway characterized here is distinct from this pathway: ts- substrates remain mitochondrial and are degraded independently of ERAD E2s or E3s .
selection_reasoning: This clarifies the spatial and mechanistic specificity of the newly characterized degradation pathway.

fact: Ubx2, previously known as an ER transmembrane protein involved in ERAD, has a discrete and functional mitochondrial pool that plays a substantial role in degradation of mitochondrial ts- substrates.
source_span: Here , we provide strong evidence for a discrete , functional , mitochondrial pool of Ubx2 ... we found another Cdc48 complex co-factor , Ubx2 , to have a substantially greater role in degradation of the two ts- substrates .
selection_reasoning: This identifies a key novel factor in mitochondrial protein quality control.

fact: Ubx2 interacts with the mitochondrial protein Fzo1 and is required for its degradation, suggesting Ubx2 may have a broad role in mitochondrial-associated degradation and mitochondrial homeostasis beyond its role in ERAD.
source_span: Interestingly , we find that Ubx2 also interacts with Fzo1 at mitochondria and is required for its degradation . This raises the interesting possibility that Ubx2 , as well as its mammalian ortholog UbxD8 , will have a broad role in MAD and mitochondrial homeostasis in addition to its role in ERAD .
selection_reasoning: This extends the significance of Ubx2 to mitochondrial protein quality control and potential conservation in mammals.

fact: The ubiquitin ligases San1 and Ubr1, which have broad roles in quality control of misfolded cytosolic and nuclear proteins, are required for degradation of mitochondrial ts- substrates.
source_span: Instead , San1 and Ubr1 , which have broad roles as quality control E3s for misfolded cytosolic and nuclear proteins ... , are required to degrade mitochondrial ts- substrates .
selection_reasoning: This identifies the ubiquitin ligases responsible for tagging mitochondrial substrates for degradation.

fact: Sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts substrates remain mitochondrial when degradation is blocked, and nuclear import factors are dispensable for their degradation, indicating degradation occurs at mitochondria rather than in the nucleus.
source_span: Sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts , however , remain mitochondrial when degradation is blocked and specific factors implicated in nuclear import were found to be dispensable .
selection_reasoning: This supports the conclusion that degradation occurs locally at mitochondria, not after nuclear import.

fact: The SSA family of Hsp70 chaperones is involved in mitochondrial ts- protein degradation, reflecting commonality with cytosolic and ER-associated degradation pathways for misfolded proteins.
source_span: For ubiquitination of QC substrates to occur , they must first be recognized as being improperly folded . In most QC systems , this recognition requires chaperones . Here , the involvement of the SSA family of Hsp70s in mitochondrial ts- protein degradation reflects commonality with cytosolic QC pathways and ERAD pathways for cytosolic misfolded domains ( ERAD-C ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact links chaperone involvement in mitochondrial quality control to broader cellular protein quality control mechanisms.

fact: Mitochondrial protein quality control (QC) requires recognition of misfolded proteins, which often depends on chaperones such as the SSA family of Hsp70s.
source_span: For ubiquitination of QC substrates to occur, they must first be recognized as being improperly folded. In most QC systems, this recognition requires chaperones. Here, the involvement of the SSA family of Hsp70s in mitochondrial ts-protein degradation reflects commonality with cytosolic QC pathways and ERAD pathways for cytosolic misfolded domains (ERAD-C).
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the biological mechanism underlying mitochondrial protein QC, which is central to the study's focus on degradation pathways.

fact: The SSA family of Hsp70 chaperones is required for co-translational folding or import of some mitochondrial proteins, positioning them to recognize misfolded mitochondrial proteins and target them for degradation by the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS).
source_span: The SSA family of chaperones is required for co-translational folding or import of at least some mitochondrial proteins (Ben-Menachem et al., 2018; Deshaies et al., 1988; Sass et al., 2003; Young et al., 2003), positioning them to play a role in recognizing misfolded mitochondrial proteins and targeting them to the UPS.
selection_reasoning: This fact provides a key mechanistic insight linking chaperones to mitochondrial protein degradation, relevant to the study's main question.

fact: The degradation of the native mitochondrial outer membrane (MOM) protein Fzo1 largely does not require Hsp70 chaperones, indicating a distinction between regulated ubiquitination and misfolded substrate degradation in mitochondria.
source_span: On the other hand, we have found that the degradation of a native MOM protein, Fzo1, largely does not require Hsp70 chaperones, extending to mitochondria a distinction between misfolded substrates and those whose ubiquitination occurs in a regulated manner.
selection_reasoning: This principal finding highlights a key difference in degradation mechanisms for native versus misfolded mitochondrial proteins.

fact: Mitochondrial inner membrane and intermembrane space (IMS) proteins have been identified as proteasome substrates, suggesting overlap and divergence with the mitochondrial quality control pathway studied here.
source_span: Several mitochondrial inner membrane and IMS proteins have also been identified as proteasome substrates (Bragoszewski et al., 2013; Margineantu et al., 2007; Pearce and Sherman, 1997; Radke et al., 2008). It now becomes of interest to ascertain how their degradation overlaps with and diverges from the QC pathway defined herein.
selection_reasoning: This fact situates the study within the broader context of mitochondrial protein degradation and motivates further research.

fact: Understanding mitochondrial protein degradation pathways in yeast may provide insights into mammalian mitochondrial protein turnover and overall mitochondrial homeostasis.
source_span: Finally, it will also be important to determine how our findings extend to mammalian mitochondrial protein turnover and mitochondrial homeostasis as a whole.

fact: Relative R0 describes thermal suitability for Ross River virus transmission and provides key temperature values: upper and lower thermal limits where transmission is possible and the temperature that maximizes transmission potential.
source_span: Relative R0 describes thermal suitability for transmission . Combined with factors like breeding habitat availability , vector control , humidity , human and reservoir host density , host immune status , and mosquito exposure , relative R0 can be used to predict disease incidence . In this approach , only the relative thermal response of each trait influences R0 , which is desirable since traits can differ substantially due to other factors and in laboratory versus field settings ( particularly mosquito survival: Clements and Paterson , 1981 ) . Relative R0 does not provide a threshold for sustained disease transmission ( i . e . where absolute R0 = 1 ) , since this threshold is not controlled solely by temperature . Instead , relative R0 preserves the temperature-dependence of R0 to provide three key temperature values: upper and lower thermal limits where transmission is possible ( R0 >0; a conservative threshold where transmission is not excluded by high or low temperatures ) and the temperature that maximizes R0 .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the key metric used to quantify temperature effects on transmission.

fact: Ross River virus incidence is often positively associated with warmer temperatures, but this relationship varies across space and time due to an intermediate thermal optimum for transmission.
source_span: RRV incidence is often—but not always—positively associated with warmer temperatures ( Tong and Hu , 2001; Tong et al . , 2002a; Tong et al . , 2004; Hu et al . , 2004; Hu et al . , 2010; Jacups et al . , 2008b , Williams et al . , 2009; Werner et al . , 2012; Koolhof et al . , 2017 ) . selection_reasoning: This fact captures a key biological insight about temperature's nonlinear effect on disease transmission.

fact: Mosquito life history traits such as biting rate, vector competence, adult mortality, parasite development rate, fecundity, egg-to-adult survival, and development rate depend on temperature and influence Ross River virus transmission.
source_span: In both equations , ( T ) indicates that a parameter depends on temperature , a is mosquito biting rate , bc is vector competence ( proportion of mosquitoes becoming infectious post-exposure ) , µ is adult mosquito mortality rate ( adult lifespan , lf = 1/µ ) , PDR is parasite development rate ( PDR = 1/EIP , the extrinsic incubation period ) , N is human density , and r is the recovery rate at which humans become immune ( all rates are measured in days−1 ) . The latter two terms do not depend on temperature . In the full R0 model , mosquito density ( M ) depends on fecundity ( EFD , eggs per female per day ) , proportion surviving from egg-to-adulthood ( pEA ) , and mosquito development rate ( MDR ) , divided by the square of adult mortality rate ( µ ) ( Parham and Michael , 2009 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact identifies the key biological traits incorporated in the transmission model.

fact: Thermal responses of mosquito traits were fit using Bayesian inference with Brière or quadratic functions to capture asymmetrical or symmetrical temperature effects.
source_span: We fit thermal responses of each trait using Bayesian inference with the ‘r2jags’ package ( Plummer , 2003; Su and Yajima , 2009 ) in R ( R Core Team , 2017 ) . Traits with asymmetrical thermal responses were fit as Brière functions: qT ( T–Tmin ) ( Tmax–T ) 1/2 ( Briere et al . , 1999 ) . Traits with symmetrical thermal responses were fit as quadratic functions: -q ( T–Tmin ) ( T–Tmax ) .
selection_reasoning: This describes the key methodological approach to modeling temperature effects on vector traits.

fact: Thermal biology principles and data from other mosquito species indicate that biting rate and parasite development rate decline at high temperatures.
source_span: Nonetheless , data from other mosquito species ( Mordecai et al . , 2013; Mordecai et al . , 2017 ) and principles of thermal biology ( Dell et al . , 2011 ) imply these traits must decline at high temperatures .
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the expected temperature-dependent behavior of key traits affecting disease transmission.

source_span: Thus , for those traits we included an artificial data point where the trait value approached zero at a very high temperature ( 40°C ) , allowing us to fit the Brière function . We used strongly informative priors to limit the effect of these traits on the upper thermal limit of R0 ( by constraining them to decline near 40°C ) .
selection_reasoning: This describes the key modeling approach used to estimate temperature-dependent transmission potential.

source_span: We used 2016 estimates for the fifteen most populous urban areas , which together contain 76 . 6% of Australia’s population ( Australian Bureau of Statistics , 2017 ) . We calculated R0 ( T ) for each location ( as above ) and estimated a population-weighted average . We compared this country-scale estimate of R0 ( T ) with data on mean monthly human cases of RRV nationwide from 1992 to 2013 obtained from the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System .
selection_reasoning: This fact connects modeled transmission potential to observed human disease incidence at a national scale.

fact: The study used mosquito fecundity and adult survival data from McDonald et al. (1980) to fit thermal response models for mosquito life-history traits.
source_span: The fecundity and adult survival data in McDonald et al . ( 1980 ) were published as time series of one experimental population at each temperature . The resulting data needed to be transformed to fit the corresponding trait thermal responses .
selection_reasoning: Using empirical life-history data to model thermal responses is a key methodological step supporting the study's main findings.

fact: Mosquito survival data were converted from percent surviving over time into lifespan data to fit thermal response models.
source_span: For survival , McDonald et al . reported the percent surviving approximately every other day ( hereafter: ‘semi-daily’ ) . We used these data—along with the number of female adults alive on the first day of oviposition at each temperature—to generate a semi-daily time series estimating the number surviving . To generate the dataset that we used to directly fit the thermal responses , we converted this time series into the number of female individuals who died on each day ( i . e . lifespan data ) .
selection_reasoning: Transforming survival data into lifespan data is a key data processing step enabling accurate thermal response modeling.

fact: Mosquito fecundity data were adjusted by binning over gonotrophic cycle durations and weighting by survival to better represent daily fecundity for thermal response fitting.
source_span: Because the population was synchronized , and because mosquitoes lay discrete clutches of eggs separated by several days ( the gonotrophic cycle duration ) , there were many data points when the populations did not produce offspring . These zero-inflated fecundity data are not ideal for fitting thermal responses . Therefore , after digitizing the semi-daily fecundity time series , we binned periods of several days ( the bin size varied by temperature , since the gonotrophic cycle duration varies with temperature ) and took a survival-weighted average within each bin ( so days with more individual mothers contributing to offspring production counted more ) . To generate the dataset that we used to directly fit the thermal responses , we weighted the values within each bin by the mean number of surviving mothers in that bin .
selection_reasoning: Adjusting fecundity data to account for mosquito reproductive biology and survival is important for accurate modeling of temperature effects on reproduction.

fact: The study used the genus name Aedes for mosquitoes despite a recent taxonomic proposal to elevate some subgenera to genus status, reflecting current consensus.
source_span: In 2000 there was a proposed shift in mosquito taxonomy: several subgenera within the genus Aedes were elevated to genus status ( Wilkerson et al . , 2015 ) . This change affected Aedes vigilax and Aedes camptorhynchus , which were called Ochlerotataus vigilax and Ochlerotatus camptorhynchus for a time by some researchers . More recently , there has been a consensus to return to the previous naming system , so we use Aedes here , although many of the papers we cite use Ochlerotatus instead .
selection_reasoning: Clarifying mosquito taxonomy is relevant background for understanding the species studied and aligning terminology with current standards.

fact: Prior studies showed that single motor cortical cells synchronize to ongoing beta oscillations but do not change their mean firing rate, only their spiking variability decreases during oscillations.
source_span: Prior studies investigating neural activity changes during beta oscillations used acute , single-electrode recording preparations and showed that single cells are synchronized to ongoing oscillations but that the strength of this synchronization is unrelated to the involvement of the neuron during the motor task ( Murthy and Fetz , 1996a ) . These studies also show individual cells do not change their mean spike firing rate but do exhibit a reduction in spiking variability during oscillations compared to the variability exhibited before the oscillation ( Murthy and Fetz , 1996b ) .
selection_reasoning: This background fact contextualizes the neural activity changes associated with beta oscillations.

fact: Three macaque monkeys were trained to perform both a standard center-out arm-reaching task and a novel sequential beta neurofeedback arm-reaching task to study beta oscillations and motor behavior.
source_span: To explore how beta oscillations reflect changes in spiking activity and movement parameters , we trained three macaque monkeys to perform a typical center-out arm-reaching task ( CO task , Figure 1a ) , and a novel sequential beta neurofeedback arm-reaching task ( NR task , Figure 1b ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the key experimental design and model organism used to investigate the study question.

fact: During the neurofeedback-reaching task, monkeys modulated their motor cortical beta band power to control a cursor and achieve targets before performing a reaching movement.
source_span: Subjects modulated endogenous motor cortical local field potential signals to move the vertical position of the beta cursor . Specifically , the cursor was controlled by a spectral estimate of beta band power normalized by a spectral estimate of broadband ( 1–100 Hz ) power ... When the beta cursor fell in the beta target , subjects were required to hold within the beta target for 450 ms . After successful completion , both the beta cursor and beta target disappeared , cueing that the reaching epoch had begun ... Subjects then executed a right-arm reach from the central target to a peripheral target to receive a liquid reward .
selection_reasoning: This fact summarizes the novel neurofeedback method linking beta oscillations to motor behavior, central to the study's approach.

fact: Monkeys improved their performance in the neurofeedback-reaching task over about one week of training and then maintained stable performance above chance levels.
source_span: When monkeys were first exposed to the task , their time to successfully complete the neurofeedback epoch improved over days . During NR task performance from these days , subjects exhibited above chance performance ...
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the learning and stable control of beta oscillations by monkeys, supporting the validity of the neurofeedback paradigm.

fact: In the neurofeedback-reaching task, monkeys modulated their motor cortical beta power to control a cursor and then performed a reaching movement to a peripheral target.
source_span: In the neurofeedback-reaching ( NR ) task monkeys performed neurofeedback immediately followed by an arm reach to a peripheral target ( Figure 1b , c ) .
selection_reasoning: Summarizes the key experimental paradigm linking neural activity modulation to motor behavior.

fact: The beta neurofeedback cursor represented an estimate of the monkey’s motor cortical beta power, updated every 100 ms, which the monkey controlled by modulating endogenous neural signals.
source_span: A yellow square beta cursor representing an estimate of the monkey’s motor cortical beta power and one of four beta targets appeared on the left of the screen . As estimates of normalized motor cortical beta power increased or decreased , the beta cursor position increased or decreased on the y axis , updating every 100 ms . Subjects modulated their endogenous neural signals to make the beta cursor hover over the beta target for 450 ms to successfully end the neurofeedback epoch .
selection_reasoning: Explains the neural signal used for neurofeedback and how it was behaviorally controlled, central to the study's method and findings.

fact: Monkeys received a liquid reward after successfully completing the neurofeedback epoch and reaching the peripheral target.
source_span: Once subjects reached the peripheral target and held for 200 ms , they received a liquid reward .
selection_reasoning: Indicates the reinforcement mechanism motivating task performance, relevant for interpreting behavioral results.

fact: The beta neurofeedback cursor was computed from local field potential signals recorded from selected motor cortex electrodes showing strong beta oscillations.
source_span: The beta neurofeedback cursor was designed to reflect endogenous beta oscillatory events in motor cortex . To calculate its position at each time point ( every 100 ms ) , LFP signals from three channels in the most anterior part of the implanted multi-electrode array were manually selected for each subject . Minimal artifacts and strong beta oscillatory activity during the reaching only task were the selection criterion , as in Engelhard et al . ( 2013 ) .
selection_reasoning: Describes the neural basis of the neurofeedback signal, important for understanding the physiological mechanism studied.

fact: Normalized beta power was calculated by dividing beta band power (25–40 Hz) by broadband power (1–100 Hz) and then mapped to cursor position on the screen.
source_span: Beta band and broadband estimates were then averaged across channels , and finally a normalized estimate of beta power ( βest ) was computed by dividing the beta band power estimate by the broadband power estimate:βest=13 ∑ch=13 ∑f=25 Hz40 Hz PSDfch13 ∑ch=13 ∑f=1 Hz100 Hz PSDfch Once βest was computed , a subject-specific linear transform was used to map βest to a vertical screen position .
selection_reasoning: Details the key signal processing step linking neural activity to the neurofeedback cursor, central to the study's methodology.

fact: Training on the beta neurofeedback task began with lenient requirements and progressed to more challenging targets as subjects improved.
source_span: Initial training began with more lenient beta neurofeedback requirements ( values to achieve low beta and high beta target were closer to the mean beta cursor value ) . As subjects improved in performance , the beta targets moved further apart until the top and bottom targets had a mean time to target of 5–10 s .
selection_reasoning: Describes the training progression, relevant for understanding how subjects learned to control beta power.

fact: A task variant required Monkey G to control the neurofeedback cursor using both normalized beta power and normalized 1–10 Hz power, increasing task complexity.
source_span: Monkey G performed one task variant of the NR task where the neurofeedback cursor in the x-axis was controlled with normalized 1–10 Hz power in addition to it being controlled in the y-axis with normalized beta power , as described above .
selection_reasoning: Highlights an experimental manipulation testing more complex neural control, relevant to the study's scope.

fact: Performance during the beta neurofeedback epoch was assessed using a target-shuffled task simulation to determine if cursor control was due to volitional modulation rather than chance fluctuations.
source_span: For each session ( typically lasting 10–40 min ) , beta cursor position from the session’s online performance was re-run through a target-shuffled task simulation , designed to assess whether the subjects’ performance during the beta neurofeedback epoch of the NR task was resulted merely from chance fluctuations in beta power or was caused by volitional changes in beta power that were specific for the beta target on the screen .
selection_reasoning: Describes a key analysis validating that neurofeedback performance reflected intentional neural modulation.

fact: The study used a simulation of a beta cursor task where success was measured by the number of beta targets acquired per session.
source_span: In the simulation , after the beta cursor entered the beta target and held for the 450 ms beta target hold time , an average arm-reaching time , the constant reward time , and the constant inter-trial interval time transpired to simulate the natural pacing of the task . At the end of the simulation , a metric of chance performance was the mean number of successful beta targets acquired over the length of the session .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the core behavioral task and performance metric used in the study, which is central to understanding the experimental design and results.

fact: Beta oscillatory events were identified by filtering local field potential signals at 25–40 Hz and applying an amplitude threshold based on the 60th percentile of rewarded trials.
source_span: To determine when the beta oscillatory events occurred , the following procedure was applied . The local field potential ( LFP ) signal from one of the electrodes used in the neurofeedback task was selected , and filtered at 25–40 Hz with a fifth order Butterworth filter . The amplitude of the filtered signal was estimated with the Hilbert transform . Each day , a distribution of amplitude values was computed by aggregating all rewarded trials from that day . A threshold was set at the 60th percentile of the resultant distribution .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the key method used to detect beta oscillations, which is fundamental to the study's analysis of neural activity.

fact: Beta oscillatory events lasting less than 125 ms were excluded to ensure that only sustained oscillations of at least 3–4 cycles were analyzed.
source_span: Then , the length of each block of uninterrupted '1s' was computed , and if the block was longer than 125 ms ( so the oscillatory episode lasted at least 3–4 cycles as described in Murthy and Fetz ( 1996a ) ; Sherman et al . , 2016 ) , the block remained as is . If the block was less than 125 ms , all points in the block were changed back to '0s' .
selection_reasoning: This fact clarifies the criteria for defining meaningful beta oscillations, which is important for interpreting the neural data.

fact: A threshold of 3.5 cm/sec hand speed was used to distinguish slow from fast movement timepoints in the study.
source_span: Throughout the study slow and fast timepoints are distinguished . A threshold of 3 . 5 cm/sec applied to hand speed was used to separate slow from fast . This threshold was chosen because using it yielded the best discrete classifier performance separating slow spiking patterns from fast spiking patterns in Monkeys G and C’s CO task in comparison with other thresholds ( data not shown ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact provides a key behavioral classification used in the analysis linking movement speed to neural activity.

fact: Movement onset time during the arm-reaching epoch was defined as the time when projected hand speed first rose above 20% of its peak value.
source_span: To compute movement onset time for the arm-reaching epoch in the NR task , we used a method inspired by Churchland and Shenoy ( 2007 ) . First , the x and y cursor velocity over the course of the reach ( t x 2 ) was projected onto a unit vector pointing from the center to peripheral target . The norm of the projected cursor velocities yielded a single time series of projected speed ( t x 1 ) . The index and value of maximum projected hand speed was computed and called ( i , M ) . Starting at i , we scanned backwards in time ( i-1 , i-2 , … ) until the value of the projected hand speed fell below 20% of the peak hand speed ( 0 . 2*M , see Figure 1f ) . This timepoint was called the movement onset time and was used because it allowed for comparisons across different reach targets , animals , and experimental setups without having to define absolute hand velocity cutoffs .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes a key method for defining movement onset, which is critical for aligning neural and behavioral data.

fact: Movement onset time was used as a standardized timepoint to compare reach behaviors across different targets, animals, and experimental setups without relying on absolute hand velocity cutoffs.

fact: Cuzick’s test for trend was used to assess whether behavioral metrics showed significant ordered changes across groups defined by beta power levels.
source_span: Cuzick’s test for trend ( Cuzick , 1985 ) is a non-parametric test for significant ordering of groups in an increasing or decreasing manner ( two-tailed ) , and was used to assess significance of ordering of behavioral metrics according to the four beta target .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes a key statistical method used to link beta power groupings to behavioral outcomes, central to the study's main analyses.

fact: Trials were grouped into quartiles based on beta power estimates to test whether movement onset times varied systematically with beta power levels.
source_span: Trials were assigned group labels according to which quartile their power estimate for a particular frequency band falls in . For Figure 5a–c , non-normalized beta is computed in a window including the last 800 ms of the neurofeedback epoch . Trials were assigned labels depending on where they fell in the distribution of non-normalized beta power across trials: 0-25th percentile: label: 1 , 25th – 50th percentile: label: 2 , 50th – 75th percentile: label: 3 , and 75th – 100th percentile: label: 4 . Then , Cuzick’s test was performed using the newly assigned labels to assess whether MOTs for non-normalized beta power exhibit the same significant ordering .
selection_reasoning: This fact summarizes the main approach to linking beta power to movement timing, a principal experimental manipulation and analysis.

fact: A logistic regression classifier was trained on spiking activity to distinguish pre-movement onset from post-movement onset periods in two different motor tasks.
source_span: To assess the information about movement onset contained in spiking activity during different parts of the NR and CO tasks, a logistic regression classifier was trained on spiking activity to discriminate pre-movement onset (PreMO) and post-movement onset (PostMO).

fact: Computational methods for predicting HIV drug resistance have become available over the last decade and can perform as well as phenotypic assays.
source_span: Conversely, various computational methods have become available over the last decade. selection_reasoning: This supports the relevance and validity of computational prediction approaches.

fact: Phenotypic assays measure HIV replication in vitro to assess drug susceptibility, expressed as Log Fold Change relative to wild type virus.
source_span: Phenotypic assays measure the replication of HIV in vitro subsequent to genotype determination. Antiretroviral drug susceptibility is expressed as the base 10 logarithm of a numerical fold change (Log FC). Log FC is determined by dividing the IC50 for inhibition of the mutated virus by the IC50 for inhibition of a determined wild type virus (wt).
selection_reasoning: This provides necessary background on how resistance is experimentally measured.

fact: VircoTYPE HIV-1 is a computational tool that predicts HIV drug resistance based on mutation presence and pairs, and has shown better clinical outcomes than phenotypic assays in a randomized trial.
source_span: In a randomized clinical trial, VircoTYPE HIV-1 has been shown to perform slightly better than conventional phenotypic assays in decreasing HIV RNA concentration over a follow up period of 48 weeks (39% of the phenotypic assay group reached HIV RNA below 400 copies/ml compared to 51% of the VircoTYPE HIV-1 group).
selection_reasoning: This illustrates the clinical utility of computational resistance prediction tools.

source_span: Next to VircoTYPE HIV-1, another implementation of a virtual phenotype has been developed at the Max Planck Institute, called Geno2Pheno. This tool has been trained on smaller dataset compared to VircoTYPE. However, it has been retrospectively validated on the Stanford HIV Drug Resistance Database (Stanford Set) in 2009. In this study Geno2Pheno outperformed state-of-the-art-expert based systems by finding 16.2–19.8% more successful regimens.
selection_reasoning: This supports the effectiveness of computational approaches in improving treatment selection.

fact: The protease inhibitor (PI) model showed the best predictive performance with an RMSE of 0.43 log units and R² of 0.76 on the Stanford dataset.

selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the principal finding about model accuracy, important for assessing clinical utility.

fact: The non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI) model had the largest prediction error due to several outliers in the data.
source_span: while the NNRTIs are predicted with the largest error ( with an RMSE of 0 . 62 log units and an R02 of 0 . 66 ) , which is the result of a number of outliers
selection_reasoning: This fact identifies limitations in model performance relevant to interpretation and future improvement.
